#7821. The Best Benchtop Planers, Tested and Reviewed

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

By Glenda Taylor, Mark Wolfe, Additional research provided by Tom Scalisi

Published Nov 9, 2026 9:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Benchtop planers—box-shaped power tools that reduce board thickness while smoothing the surface—top many a woodcrafter’s wish list. They fine-tune the wood used to create cabinets, bookshelves, and more, replacing old-fashioned hand planes because they’re much faster and easier to use.

Like our readers, we wanted to know which of today’s popular models perform well in real workshop situations, so we tested them. We selected highly rated benchtop planers and started planing boards—hundreds of ’em! We also reached out to Jay Sanders, licensed contractor and owner of Castle Dream Construction, a home remodeling company based in Baltimore, Maryland, to get his insights on what to consider when shopping for one.

After testing, we liked the 15-amp DeWalt 13-Inch 3-Knife 2-Speed Thickness Planer the best. We chose it based on its built-in infeed and outfeed tables, fan-assisted chip ejection vacuums, and impressive speed.

Keep reading to find out how the following models earned a spot in this lineup of the best benchtop planers for DIYers and seasoned woodworkers.

Bottom line: Our tests reveal top benchtop planers for various needs, with DeWalt leading for overall performance and versatility.

Investing in the right benchtop planer is important for anyone who’s into woodworking. We put the top DIY and professional models through their paces and scrutinized each. The models that earned a spot in our lineup are among the best benchtop thickness planers available today, so one is likely to find a favored place in your workshop.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5; Performance 5/5; Board Capacity 5/5; Dust 4.7/5; Value 4.8/5

Those in the market for a high-capacity planer with plenty of features will want to consider the DeWalt 13-inch thickness planer. This benchtop planer can handle materials up to a 13-inch width capacity with a 6-inch length. This heavy planer weighs in at 92 pounds, and we found its weight was beneficial in keeping it in one place during operation. We put the planer on a reinforced work surface—this tool is too heavy for most portable-type bolt holes in the base.

We’re familiar with the high quality of many DeWalt tools, and this thickness planer is no exception. It boasts a powerful 15-amp motor and a three-blade cutterhead that spins at 10,000 revolutions per minute (rpm). It can be set to plane off as much as ⅛ inch of wood in a single pass. It comes standard with front and back stainless steel infeed and outfeed tables that help support the boards as they pass through the planer. A unique option on this benchtop planer is the ability to adjust the feed speed. A lever on the front let us select either 96 or 179 cuts per inch (cpi). At 95 cpi, the DeWalt planer pulled the boards through twice as quickly as when we selected 179 cpi, but the surface was slightly rougher. Interestingly, even at 96 cpi, we found the boards were smooth enough for most high-end woodworking. At 179 cpi, they felt as though they’d already been sanded. This is in large part because of the three straight blades in the DeWalt planer. Most of today’s planers have only two blades.

We planed dozens of boards with the DeWalt model: softwoods, including pine and cedar; and hardwoods, including ash, oak, and walnut. The DeWalt planed all of them smoothly, and we found little to no snipe on any of the boards. We attributed this benefit to an extension outfeed table that helps support the boards as they exit the machine. The benchtop planer has a fan-assisted chip-ejection port on the back of the machine that we connected to our dust-collection system. The chip-ejection fan is so powerful that when we walked behind the machine to grab the board as it passed through, the chips stung when they hit us. Impressive! And slightly painful. The downside is that the chip-ejection port is positioned just over the outfeed table, so the hose on our dust-collection system kept dipping down and interfering with the boards as they exited the planer. Our makeshift fix was to tie the hose up to keep it out of the way.

We believe this top-notch planer would be an asset in any DIYer or woodcrafter’s shop. It’s powerful, the feed speed is adjustable, and the ruler gauge is accurate. (We measured the planed boards with calipers to determine gauge accuracy.) The model comes with a “bump” on/off switch in the front that allowed us to shut the machine down simply by bumping the switch with our hand or arm. This is a safety feature in the event something goes wrong—such as a board getting caught sideways or an article of clothing getting drawn into the machine. Just a bump, and the DeWalt shuts down.

What our tester says: “I am a firm believer in ‘buy it once, use it forever,’ and the DeWalt DW735 feels like that kind of tool. Hardwood, softwood, fresh and sappy or old and dried boards, the finished faces always come out clean and smooth.”—Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews writer and tester

See our full review: DeWalt 13-Inch 3-Knife 2-Speed Thickness Planer

Get the DeWalt benchtop planer at Amazon, Lowe’s, or The Home Depot.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4.5/5; Performance 4/5; Board Capacity 4.5/5; Dust 4.5/5; Value 4.8/5

As a reasonably priced wood planer that can handle up to 12.25-inch-wide boards, the Craftsman benchtop thickness planer is worth a look. The manufacturer has a long and reputable history of making durable tools and quality machines. At just 61.8 pounds, the Craftsman was a bit easier to lift and position on the work surface, but we noted that this lighter weight resulted in the machine “walking” just a bit when we planed large hardwood boards. Fortunately, there’s a simple solution: Just bolt it down to a workbench. The benchtop planer has a 15-amp motor that produces cutter speeds up to 8,000 rpm. Thanks to its two-blade straight-knife cutter design, it provides 16,000 cuts per minute, which we found to be more than adequate for most small cabinetry and furniture-building projects.

This Craftsman planer accepts boards up to 6 inches long, and it comes with a safety bump on/off switch on the front and a precision gauge along the side for selecting the correct cutting height. The planer removes up to ⅛ inch. The Craftsman doesn’t offer a feed-speed adjustment, and we couldn’t find a feed-speed rating listed in the owner’s manual, but we used a stopwatch and came up with an approximate feed speed of 23 feet per minute. The planed boards were smooth enough that a light sanding would remove any residual grain roughness, but we did find a 2-inch snipe at the end of every board we planed. This is a common occurrence with planers; we didn’t deduct any points—just be aware that it occurs and plan to plane boards a couple of inches longer than the desired finished length. Those who won’t use a benchtop planer often and are a bit short on space might appreciate the fold-up infeed and outfeed tables that make storage a bit easier. We found this handy for setting the planer out of the way under a table.

Get the Craftsman benchtop planer at Amazon or Lowe’s.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4.7/5; Performance 4.7/5; Board Capacity 5/5; Dust 3/5; Value 4.5/5

Anyone looking for a portable planer that provides extra maximum thickness—for timber frame mailbox posts, say, or heavy furniture—will want to check out the 2012NB 12-inch planer from Makita. This machine has an above-average 6 3/32-inch maximum thickness capacity, which is slightly higher than the others we tested. The real draw of the Makita 2012NB comes in its stability and quiet operation. It’s remarkably stable for its relatively light weight of just 61.9 pounds. It didn’t walk or shift, even when we ran large hardwood boards through, making it one of the best portable thickness planers that do need to be bolted down. Plus, though hearing protection is still recommended, it’s noticeably quieter than the other models we tested—a sound output of 83 decibels, according to the manufacturer. The other planers don’t list the decibel factor but were, in our estimation, about a quarter louder than the Makita.

This planer has a 15-amp motor that produces 8,500 rpm on the cutterhead. It has two straight-knife cutters and a cutting depth of up to 1/8 inch. The Interna-Lok head clamp holds the board in place better than standard rollers, and we didn’t find any snipe on boards shorter than 4 feet long. As we planed longer boards, however, we began to see a faint snipe line on the last 2 inches of the board. By supporting the end of the board as it came out, we could eliminate the snipe line. Whether we removed 1/8 inch or 1/64 inch, the planed boards came out very smooth and would need only light sanding for most projects.

The feed speed is not adjustable, but the Makita makes quick work of pulling the boards through—the manufacturer lists the feed rate as 27.9 feet per minute, which seemed about right in our tests, but keep in mind that heavy boards typically move slightly slower than small lightweight boards. The planer comes with a bump power switch and a precision gauge, and although it doesn’t have a built-in dust-collection port, an attachment is sold separately.

Get the Makita benchtop planer at Amazon, The Home Depot, or Ace Tool.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4.5/5; Performance 4/5; Board Capacity 4.5/5; Dust 4/5; Value 4.2/5

Those looking for a robust planer for resurfacing rough or reclaimed lumber, or smoothing and thinning new lumber, may want to consider the Wen benchtop thickness planer. We found this model well suited to removing up to 1/8 inch of wood from the surface of boards up to 12.5 inches wide. In addition, it handles board heights of up to 6 inches. With 10,000 rpm, this planer offers plenty of power for smoothing rough wood. Its two straight blades make up to 20,000 cuts per minute. The height adjustment handle on this planer is slightly smaller than some—and it’s located at the top of the machine—but it still follows the same general rule of one turn equals 1/16 inch.

When we planed the first board on the Wen and then measured it for precision, we found it was 1/32 inch too high. That may not sound like a lot, but it’s substantial when it comes to creating uniform board height for a project. Fortunately, the gauge is adjustable, so we used a small screwdriver to adjust it 1/32 inch and then ran another board through. Perfect! Most planer gauges come preset, but occasionally one can be slightly off. Just adjust it and try again. We did notice some snipe at the last couple of inches, so we recommend planing boards at least 2 inches longer than needed. There’s no feed-speed adjustment, but according to the manufacturer, the planer moves boards as quickly as 26 feet per minute, depending on size.

At just 55.6 pounds, the Wen is slightly on the light side, and we needed to bolt it down to keep it from moving during operation. It comes with a conveniently located port that we attached to our dust-collection system. We did notice some small chips remained on the feed plate after planing. This isn’t a big issue, but the ejection fan didn’t seem to eject all of them through the port. If necessary, this can be remedied by just blowing the chips out before inserting a new board. Like many other quality planers, the Wen has a bump-type on/off switch for added safety.

Get the Wen benchtop planer at Amazon, Lowe’s, or The Home Depot.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4/5; Performance 4/5; Board Capacity 4.5/5; Dust 4/5; Value 4.3/5

Besides our Best Overall pick, the Ridgid 13-inch planer is the only other three-blade planer we tested, and it impressed us on many fronts. It features a maximum cut allowance of ⅛ inch and accepts boards up to 13 inches wide and 6⅛ inches high. In addition to its gauge, which is easy to read and comes with 1/64-inch increments, it also features a separate Ind-I-Cut gauge on the front of the planer that allowed us to see exactly how much wood we were removing in a pass. We found this feature valuable, especially because tiny 1/64-inch increments can be challenging to see. The Ind-I-Cut acted like a magnifying glass to let us see the amount of wood we were removing as we planned. The Ridgid planer features 9,000 rpm at the cutterhead, which translates into 27,000 cuts per minute, an enviable number of cuts in the world of planers.

We tested it on dozens of boards, both hardwood and softwood species, large and small, and it powered through all of them without bogging down. We did get a little snipe at the ends of the boards, but given how much power—and how smooth—the Ridgid performs, it was a minor downside. We found that supporting the ejected boards helped lessen, but didn’t fully eliminate, the snipe. As with the other planers we tested, we appreciated the large bump on/off switch for safety. At 73 pounds, the Ridgid remained firmly rooted while we planed board after board. It features a chip-ejector port that connects to a standard dust-collection system.

This planer is suitable for removing rough, weathered surface grain as well as fine-tuning hardwood for furniture and cabinetry projects. Its third blade and its Ind-I-Cut gauge pretty much puts it in a class by itself. Those who want an aggressive three-blade planer but don’t want to spend the extra bucks may wish to consider the Ridgid planer. We were delighted with its performance.

Get the Ridgid benchtop planer at The Home Depot.

When selecting the best benchtop planers, Sanders considers several factors, including cutterhead type, power, and whether the benchtop planer comes with a table that supports the boards. We looked at all of these factors during the selection process, plus we considered how well each planer rated with experienced users. We also considered the brand to an extent. After all, manufacturers such as DeWalt, Makita, and Craftsman have top-notch reputations in the power tool industry. We didn’t stick with just those three; we also included additional highly rated models from other manufacturers.

We unboxed and set up the benchtop planers according to manufacturer specifications. Then, we started planing new wood, reclaimed wood, softwood boards, and hardwood boards. We paid special attention to how smooth the planers left the board surfaces and whether the machines left snipes (unwanted cuts in the last few inches of the board).

We analyzed overall performance and ease of use and awarded points based on a rubric. The better a planer performed, the higher the points. After testing, we averaged the points to help determine the best category and intended use.

Benchtop planers, also known as “thickness planers” because they reduce the thickness of a board, have rotating blades inside that shave off a thin layer of wood. Those who are interested in owning one but don’t have a lot of experience with this powerful tool will want to keep the following factors and features in mind when shopping.

A benchtop planer’s motor needs enough power to get the job done. How much is enough depends on specific projects.

If users work primarily with softer woods such as pine, cedar, and fir—for building country-style furniture or birdhouses, for example—a motor in the 1- to 1½-horsepower (hp) range might suit them well. A thickness planer doesn’t need much juice to shave a layer off the top of these materials.

However, if users are into high-end joinery or cabinetry, they’ll probably work with species such as oak, maple, and even walnut. These hard materials will require more from a planer to shave them down, so they’ll want to look for a 2 hp tool.

Perhaps even more important than horsepower is a planer’s motor rating—choose one with a 15-amp motor. Planers draw a lot of electricity, and Sanders suggests getting a powerful one. “Look for at least a 15-amp motor with multiple speed options,” he advises. A 15-amp motor helps ensure the machine can handle the task without breaking down. Smaller-amperage motors don’t have the power necessary for planing wood.

Thickness planer blades (or knives) come in different styles. “The three main options are straight knife, helical, and spiral/helix,” Sanders says. “The straight knife is the most affordable but produces more tear-out. Helical and spiral cut cleaner but cost more upfront. Spiral cutter heads are generally regarded as producing the best finish.”

Blades vary on straight-knife cutter models. Some are reversible, so when they become dull, the user can turn them over and use the other side. Others have only one sharp edge, but they can be manually sharpened with a standard sharpening stone, just like a kitchen knife. Reversible knives are disposable, meant to be tossed out after both sides wear down.

All the planers we tested came with cutterheads designed to accept straight blades.

Cutting depth refers to how much material a wood planer can remove in one pass. Generally speaking, the more powerful the planer, the more material it can remove in one pass and the larger the depth of cut.

Planers that can shave off up to ⅛ inch at a time are good for removing the surface of rough or weathered wood. Removing that much depth at once, however, isn’t always optimal. Generally, it’s usually best for the board—and for the machine—to err on the side of caution and plane off thinner amounts. The more wood a planer removes in a pass, the harder it must work, which can lead to overheating if the user is planing a lot of boards.

Many woodworkers will find little need to remove more than 1/16 inch per pass, and for fine-tuning boards, they will remove even less—1/32 or 1/64 inch. Don’t pass up a planer just because it doesn’t remove ⅛ inch per pass. It’s easy enough to set the planer at 1/16 inch and then run it through twice.

A thickness planer’s allowance indicates the widest (and tallest) board that can be passed through the tool. Manufacturers label most planers with ranges between 12 inches and 13 inches (plenty for most woodworking hobbyists), but this metric doesn’t tell the whole story.

For example, a 12-inch planer can handle a board 12 inches in width capacity, but that does not say how thick (i.e., tall) a piece of wood the planer can handle. This metric is quite helpful, so look for a model that can handle materials as thick as 5 or 6 inches to get the most use out of a wood planer.

Snipe refers to an undesirable line, which can sometimes be very noticeable, left on the top end of a board after planing. It’s the result of the wood planer removing more wood at the end of the board. As the end of the board clears the first set of rollers, gravity tends to pull the board downward, which puts pressure on the other end. When this happens, the cutterhead blades may remove slightly more wood at the very end. A snipe looks like a thin dip, usually less than 1/16 inch, located along the last couple inches of the board.

“Longer infeed and outfeed tables help support boards and minimize snipe,” Sanders explains. He adds that “36-inch to 44-inch tables are good for a benchtop planer.” Just make sure they fold down for storage. Snipe may be unavoidable to some degree, but some benchtop thickness planers do better than others at minimizing its effect. A good way to avoid snipe appearing on a  finished product is to leave boards longer than necessary by an inch or so when planning and then cut the sniped ends off before using the board for your project.

Shaving the intended amount of wood off your workpieces can be tedious. Bringing a hardwood board from a 1-inch thickness to a ⅝-inch thickness, for example, could take five or six passes. The user could measure the board’s thickness before each pass and adjust the cutterhead using a tape measure or a combination square, but that’s time-consuming.

Many of today’s benchtop planers have a built-in gauge that looks like a ruler attached to the side of the intake slot. The gauge will indicate the proposed board thickness as the user raises or lowers the planer’s carriage (the top part of the tool that moves up and down) via a hand crank.

Planer gauges typically show measurements in 1/16-inch increments, but some show measurements in 1/64-inch increments. Some experienced woodworkers don’t use the gauge at all but rather determine cutting depth with the tool’s hand crank. On a planer, a complete revolution of its hand crank equals 1/16 inch. Half a crank equals 1/32 inch, and a quarter of a crank equals 1/64 inch.

A depth stop is a feature that keeps the user from shaving off more than the machine’s maximum cutting depth. For example, if the planer has a maximum cutting depth of ⅛ inch, the depth stop will prevent the user from inserting any board more than ⅛ inch thicker than the thickness chosen on the gauge (ruler). The board simply will not go into the slot. In this way, users needn’t worry about taking off more than the maximum cutting depth because the depth stop won’t allow it.

Thickness planers create a good deal of dust and wood chips. These machines rip off and spit out tiny pieces of wood, and the floor under a thickness planer will resemble a child’s sandbox after only a few boards.

Many of today’s benchtop planers have dust ports that attach to a shop vacuum or dust-collection system to minimize the mess. These collection systems also do a good job of removing the dust from the machine before it can settle in the cutterhead, helping to maintain its usable life and cutting speed.

Different speeds apply to a benchtop planer: cutterhead speed, cutting speed, and feed speed.

Alongside other popular power tools, such as band saws, table saws, and wood lathes, benchtop thickness planers are a boon in a woodworking shop. If this is your first planer, you will probably have questions about the tool’s best use and operation. Ahead are answers to some of the most common questions about benchtop planers. If you still want more information about your benchtop planer, refer to the user’s manual or contact the manufacturer.

Similar to hand planes, benchtop planers reduce the thickness of a board. Woodcrafters can use them to create consistent thicknesses on several boards for woodworking purposes or to uncover the beauty hidden underneath reclaimed wood.

With the benchtop planer turned off, place a board in the intake feed slot. Lower the roller carriage (the top part of the planer) using the hand crank until it just touches the board. This is the starting point. Remove the board, and then use the crank to lower the roller carriage to the desired cutting depth (typically between 1/64 and ⅛ inch). The woodworker can use the ruler gauge to determine the cutting depth or use the crank rule of thumb—one full revolution of the crank equals 1/16 inch. Once the cutting height is decided, turn the planer on and slowly feed the board into the intake slot. The planer will do the rest—users don’t have to push the board.

Planers reduce the thickness of a board by shaving a uniform amount of wood off its surface. Jointers make the board flat by shaving away only the high spots, not the entire surface, as a planer does.

Wood planers can be some of the heaviest tools in your shop. Benchtop planers weigh an average of between 60 and 100 pounds, so it may be wise to keep it on a benchtop rather than moving it around.

#7820. The Best Holiday Decorations Across the U.S., and How to Steal the Look

These homes are full of ideas you can borrow for your own yard.

Outdoor holiday decorating is an art. And while we love a tasteful string of white Christmas lights or a few pumpkins placed by the front door, why not really go for it when the holiday season rolls around? Over-the-top outdoor holiday decorations make the whole neighborhood get in the festive spirit! To help inspire you, we found some of the best maximalist holiday homes from coast to coast.

From extra spooky Halloween displays to dazzling Christmas spectacles, these homes are full of ideas you can borrow for your own yard.

A post shared by jessica archibald (@jessicarchibald)

Halloween 2026 has come and gone, but it’s never too early to start thinking about next year! Known simply as The Pumpkin House, @jessicarchibald lines her roof, porch, and yard with hundreds of jack-o’-lanterns every Halloween season. The piles of pumpkins make a big impact both during the day and at night.

Steal This Idea: All you need is pumpkins! Attach faux pumpkins to long boards to make them easier to display on the roof.

The Kraken House (@krakenhousenola) captured here by @amournola, uses blow-up decor to explore the haunted seas. The blow-up tentacles hint at a sea monster hiding beyond the windows, but the dramatic lighting is what really makes this house shine.

Steal This Idea: Skip the kid-friendly Bluey holiday inflatable this year, and attach these terrifying tentacles instead. Then turn up the drama with solar up-lights in green and purple.

Can you believe this amazing black cat is a DIY project? To transform this front porch into a Halloween stage, @allset_bygabrielle hand-carved the cat figure out of wood and painted every detail.

Steal This Idea: In addition to the vintage-inspired cat, the spooky forest framing the door was made with a mix of dead branches and faux botanicals; providing texture and a subtle sparkle.

This front entry in New York City (photographed by @victoria.nycvisit) uses dark drapery, black roses, and a wide variety of unique pumpkins and squashes to create a gothic masterpiece. Trick-or-treaters beware!

Steal This Idea: It’s amazing what a few swathes of black and burgundy fabric can do. Drape the fabric around your front door to make an eerie entrance. Then use pumpkins and vases full of dark flowers to complete the look.

This viral townhouse @stoopandthecity, is dressed to the nines for every holiday. This autumn harvest display features patterned pumpkins and cascades of fall foliage. It’s perfect for Thanksgiving or for those that prefer to skip the ghosts and goblins.

Steal This Idea: Choose faux and glass pumpkins in a cohesive color scheme, and don’t hold back on the fall foliage. Use faux stems to make the display last all season long.

A post shared by Marissa Fiala | Houston, TX (@houstonhotspots)

When it comes to Christmas lights, you can’t find much better than the extravagant homes in the River Oaks neighborhood of Houston, Texas. Each home goes all out with sparkling lights on its exterior, wrapped around every tree.

Steal This Idea: The secret to this colorful tree, captured by @houstonhotspots, is wrapping the lights tightly around the trunk and every single branch. The technique takes time but makes a big impact. Use LED lights to cut back on electricity use.

This famous house on Castro Street in San Francisco does not hold back! (Photo by @415urbanadventures.) Every exterior surface is covered in decor. The symmetrical layout keeps it looking classy instead of gaudy. And of course, the star of the show is Santa hanging in the middle, ready to deliver gifts.

Steal This Idea: The key element of this display is the garland covered in shiny Christmas ornaments. When you think you’ve gathered enough baubles, you’ll probably need even more!

The historic mill in Clifton, Ohio, is known for its over-the-top Christmas light display, featuring over four million lights! While you might not have a historic mill to decorate, the lighting techniques can be used on your own home to dazzle the entire neighborhood.

Steal This Idea: The most memorable element of this display is the iconic red lights cascading down the hillside. Try laying strings lights in rows along your entire yard to get a similar look.

A post shared by Joe Yost | Yost Team -Compass Pittsburgh (@joeyostteam)

Make your house look like one giant Christmas present by adding a larger-than-life red bow. This Pittsburgh mansion is famous for its red Christmas bow that looks beautifully whimsical in the daytime and lights up at night.

Steal This Idea: You don’t need a mansion to recreate this look. Get your own giant red bow and hang it above your front door. Here’s one available on Etsy!

A post shared by Pink Dreams Collection (@pinkdreamscollection)

One way to set your house apart for Christmas is to use a non-traditional color scheme —like pink! This darling cottage from @pinkdreamcollection is a frosted pink confection complete with pink trees and pink nutcracker figurines.

Steal This Idea: Pink or pastel Christmas decor will make your home look playful and unique. Use different shades of pink to add dimension.

A post shared by The Hazard’s Gingerbread House (@hazardsgingerbreadhouse)

This spectacular residential light display by Walter Hazard (@hazardsgingerbreadhouse) makes his home look like a technicolor gingerbread house. The secret is the wire-fencing frames he uses to create methodical light patterns. Visitors come from all over the area to witness the gorgeous lights in action.

Steal This Idea: We might not all have the same light-manipulation talent as Walter, but you can get the same grid-like coverage with LED curtain lights like these.

#7819. The Best Roof Rakes of 2026, Expert-Tested and Reviewed

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

By Zach Lazzari, Additional research provided by Glenda Taylor, Timothy Dale

Published Nov 9, 2026 9:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

According to the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), one foot of wet snow can weigh as much as 21 pounds per square foot—and that weight is exactly why using a roof rake can be essential to prevent damage.

To help you find the right tool for the job, we tested a range of different rakes on a tall shed and a camper after heavy snowfalls in Montana, working on metal and shingle roofs with different heights and pitches. Our favorite was the combo pack from Avalanche! since it can handle large amounts of snow and includes built-in wheels to prevent damage. Plus, it comes with different heads for different needs.

Keep reading to learn more about that model and the rest of the best roof rake options available.

Bottom line: Choosing the right roof rake can prevent damage and ensure safety during snow removal. Explore top picks and expert advice for the best options.

Note that roof rakes are intended for snow removal on single-story homes only. They should only be used when standing on the ground, and never while standing on a ladder. Attempting to balance a long pole while navigating snow-slick ladder rungs is a surefire way to slip and fall. Even if you have great balance, the weight of the snow you’re pulling off the roof could easily knock you off a ladder.

Selected for quality, functionality, material construction, and design, all of these tested products are excellent options for keeping the roof snow-free during the winter.

Equipped with a retractable plastic slide for enhanced efficiency, this rake pulls dislodged snow down the slide and off the roof, saving users time and effort. It’s also equipped with small wheels to help it glide along the roof without damaging it.

The rake extends from 4 to 15.5 feet when each fiberglass extension bar is attached. This process is simple, but it takes a few minutes to add each extension. With telescoping models being the exception, most other roof rakes use fitted extension segments similarly.

When adding an extension pole, users might need to remove gloves to press the locking button. I really liked the fiberglass poles because they aren’t nearly as cold as metal options. It is important to ensure that the segments are seated well at each joint, with the locking button in place.

Super durable, the plastic head is up to heavy-duty challenges. Raking snow off a roof is usually awkward with any rake, and that was the case with this one. But I didn’t mind a small amount of extra weight while reaching for the high spots because the durable design also gave me the confidence to hit the heavy snow spots and pull hard. I felt like the fiberglass poles were strong as well.

One other reason this won our top spot is the fact that multiple heads are included for different needs. The head that’s equipped with wheels and a slide should be able to tackle most users’ needs. The slide allows snow to fall off the roof easily, creating a pathway over gutters and other obstacles. When users hit stubborn areas and need a head that can bust through ice and grab big chunks of snow over shingles, asphalt, and tricky surfaces, they’ll want to use the rake head with wheels.

Testing was done throughout a weeklong storm event. The first 3 days received heavy snowfall with a mix of dry powder and wet snow. The powder wasn’t problematic, but the wet snow was heavy, and it stuck to the rooftops. It also underwent a slight thaw and a subsequent freeze cycle that solidified the rooftop snow.

I waited for the storm to end and rotated through each roof rake, pulling sections of snow down. I judged each roof rake based on ease of assembly, grip, length, and ability to reach and grab snow without damaging the roof. Durability was also considered. Several of the brands have similar design features with slight variations in the way they are constructed. There was a reasonable overlap when it comes to performance and function with these look-alike models.

Make sure you’re up to date on the most important product factors before deciding on the best option to rake snow from your roof and prevent ice dams from forming. Some factors to consider in finding the right snow rake for roof cleaning include the type and quality of the materials, length, weight, and head design.

A roof rake for snow removal can be made of different materials, including fiberglass, polyethylene, aluminum, and wood.

Most roof rakes come with adjustable poles that can be lengthened from 14 to 22 feet for snow removal and shortened to less than 8 feet for storage. The longer the pole, the higher users will be able to reach on the roof, but longer poles can also be unwieldy and may require more physical strength to lift and maneuver.

Roof rakes range in weight between 4 and 14 pounds, with most of the weight in the rake head. The heavier the rake head, the more likely it is to sink deeply into the snow on the roof, allowing users to remove a good amount with each pull. Conversely, heavy roof rakes require more physical strength to lift and position.

Roof rake heads range in depth from a narrow 3 inches to a generous 10 inches, and widths run between 12 and 24 inches. The larger the rake head, the more snow the rake can remove in a single pull. If the snow is wet and heavy, it can require additional physical strength to pull it, which can lead to back and shoulder fatigue.

Curved heads and interchangeable attachments, such as a scoop, blade, or plastic slide, can greatly decrease fatigue if used properly. It’s also a good idea to consider looking for a roof rake with built-in wheels or bumpers to help protect the roof and shingles from damage. This is especially important when working with an aluminum rake head or if the rake has a blade attachment.

When starting to rake the snow off of a roof, it’s important to begin the process by removing the snow from the roof’s edge first. If users attempt to extend the roof rake as much as possible and simply pull down any snow caught within this range, there is a good chance that they will be unable to move the snow. Also, keep in mind that even if the snow does move, it isn’t a good idea to bring down that much snow at once because the weight of the snow could cause injury.

While the goal of snow removal on a driveway is to clear any snow or ice that could cause the car to slip, it’s not actually necessary to rake every inch of snow off the roof. Leaving one or two inches of snow isn’t going to cause ice dams to form, and this gap can help prevent the roof shingles from being damaged during raking.

Additionally, under no circumstances should users attempt to climb a ladder or walk on a sloped roof in winter conditions to remove snow. The entire purpose of a roof rake is for the user to remain on the ground, so don’t risk trying to rake the roof while perched on a ladder.

For more information on the best roof rake for snow removal at your home, take a look at some of the most commonly asked questions and the detailed answers below.

Unlike general-purpose rakes, snow rakes (also known as roof rakes) are specially designed for one purpose: to remove snow from single-story roofs without having to climb. This makes it much easier and safer to keep the roof clear of snow and prevent ice dams from forming in the gutter system.

The blade on a roof rake head can damage the shingles on a roof. This is especially true with aluminum rake heads, but this problem can be avoided if you invest in a roof rake with built-in wheels. These wheels elevate the rake slightly, suspending the rake head above the surface of the shingles instead of grating against them.

If you rake the roof the same day it snows, you can prevent ice build-up in the gutter system.

Whether or not you need a roof rake depends on how much snow naturally builds up on your roof. Some houses have steep roofs that don’t collect a lot of snow, while others may have a gentle slope. Metal roofs can be raked with a roof rake to keep them clear of snow, but in most cases, the snow will tend to slide off a metal roof without a problem. In fact, many homes with metal roofs need snow guards or snow fences to prevent piles of snow from sliding off and potentially hurting anyone standing nearby.

It’s a good idea to rake the roof on the same day it snows, just as it isn’t wise to wait long to shovel your driveway. Keep in mind that freshly fallen snow is much easier to move than snow that has been allowed to melt and refreeze under the sun.

#7818. Former judge accused of shooting gun toward unwanted trick-or-treaters

Former Oklahoma Judge Jerry Herberger was arrested recently after allegedly shooting a gun toward unwanted trick-or-treaters. (Photo from the Stephens County Sheriff’s Office)

A former Oklahoma judge was arrested recently after allegedly shooting a gun toward unwanted trick-or-treaters who came near his home on Halloween.

Former Judge Jerry Herberger, 73, of Duncan, Oklahoma, was booked in the Stephens County Jail in Oklahoma for assault and battery with a deadly weapon, attempted murder and possession of a firearm while intoxicated, the Lawton Constitution reports.

Police were called Saturday night after witnesses said an intoxicated Herberger had threatened trick-or-treaters if they came to his home. With a gun in his hand, he allegedly fired off a round in the children’s direction, according to the Lawton Constitution.

As officers prepared to make contact at the home, Herberger allegedly pointed a gun at one of the officers, said Loisdawn Jones, the director of communications for the city of Duncan, Oklahoma. He then complied with officers’ commands and exited the residence, where he was taken into custody and booked into the Stephens County Jail.

#7816. That Hole in Your Ruler Isn’t Random – Here’s What It’s Actually For

That small hole on a ruler has a practical purpose and an unexpected history. Here's why it exists and how people use it.

Almost everyone has used a ruler at some point, whether it was for a school project, measuring something around the house, or drawing a straight line. But even after years of using one, there’s a small detail that’s easy to miss: the hole near the end.

Those holes in rulers aren’t just part of the design. They actually serve a purpose, and the reason they’re there goes back further than most people might expect. Here’s what they’re for, how they were used in the past, and a few other ways they come in handy.

The hole at the end of a ruler is mainly there for storage. It lets people hang the ruler on a hook, nail, or pegboard instead of leaving it in a drawer or on a workbench. This is particularly helpful with longer metal rulers that might not fit in a toolbox.

But the hole has been around for much longer than modern workshops. Years ago, before paper notebooks became common in schools, students practiced writing on small slate boards. They could wipe away their writing with a damp cloth and use the board again.

Some students tied that cloth to their rulers with a piece of string through the hole. That way, they always had something nearby to clean their slates. Schools eventually moved away from slate boards, but the holes remained. Today, they’re mostly there to make rulers easier to hang and store.

Hanging a ruler isn’t the only reason manufacturers add holes. Some rulers have several, and they can serve different purposes depending on where they’re placed. For example, certain school rulers have three holes spaced along one side. These line up with the rings in a standard three-ring binder, so students can keep their rulers with their other school supplies.

Some rulers also have holes that help with drawing circles. A pin through one hole can hold the ruler in place while a pencil in another hole traces a circle as the ruler turns. Not every ruler has holes designed for this, but specialty models like the Creative Grids Quick Trim Ruler do. A compass is still a better choice when exact measurements matter.

Some crafting rulers have holes for more specific jobs. Quilting rulers and templates may have openings that help mark circles or line up fabric before cutting. Others have slots or shaped edges that guide a rotary cutter, making it easier to cut certain shapes.

There are also special rulers for paper crafts and stitching. Some have rows of tiny, evenly spaced holes that help people mark where to make stitches or decorative patterns.

Of course, not every ruler has holes. Smaller plastic rulers often don’t need them, while longer metal versions may have one at each end. It mostly comes down to how the manufacturer expects people to use the ruler. And for everyday measuring, the holes don’t make much difference. A ruler without them can measure just as accurately as one with them.

#7813. Winter Storm Watch vs. Winter Storm Warning: What’s the Difference?

A winter storm watch and winter storm warning mean different things. Here's what each alert signals and how to prepare for dangerous weather.

Tracking severe weather can sometimes feel like it requires a degree in meteorology. With complex scientific terms and technical jargon, it can be difficult to understand what it all means and what should be done to prepare. That’s when the difference between a winter storm watch and a winter storm warning matters.

Both alerts come from the National Weather Service, but they call for different levels of urgency. Here’s how the alerts work and what homeowners should do when they see one.

A winter storm watch means a significant winter storm is possible, but forecasters aren’t yet sure where or when it will hit or how severe it will be. According to the National Weather Service, watches often arrive a day or two before a storm and can cover heavy snow, sleet, or ice.

They give residents time to prepare, even though the storm may not reach their area. As the forecast becomes clearer, the National Weather Service may upgrade the watch to a warning, issue an advisory, or cancel it altogether.

A winter storm warning means dangerous winter weather is expected or already happening. Heavy snow, sleet, or ice could make travel unsafe and cause other problems, including power outages. The amount of snow or ice needed to trigger a warning varies by location.

“Each office knows the local area and will issue Warnings, Watches or Advisories based on local criteria,” according to the National Weather Service. “For example, the amount of snow that triggers a ‘Winter Storm Warning’ in the Northern Plains is typically much higher than the amount needed to trigger a ‘Winter Storm Warning’ in the Southeast.”

Warnings generally arrive closer to a storm’s arrival than watches, although forecasters can issue one before snow or ice begins falling.

A winter weather advisory means snow, sleet, or ice is expected to cause problems, but forecasters don’t anticipate conditions severe enough for a warning. An advisory may signal slick roads or other travel disruptions. While the weather may be less severe than during a warning, residents should still take precautions and monitor local forecasts.

A winter storm watch gives homeowners time to prepare before conditions worsen. That includes checking heating systems, protecting exposed pipes from freezing, and stocking up on food, medications, and other essentials.

“Your primary concerns at home or work during a winter storm are loss of heat, power and telephone service and a shortage of supplies if storm conditions continue for more than a day,” according to the National Weather Service.

Homeowners should have flashlights, spare batteries, and a charged phone in case the power goes out. Checking smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, locating snow shovels, and stocking up on ice melt can also help.

Once a warning takes effect, homeowners should finish their preparations and avoid unnecessary travel. Staying indoors is generally safest during severe winter weather.

If the power goes out, residents can close off unused rooms and wear extra layers to stay warm. Portable generators should always remain outdoors, away from windows and doors. Grills and ovens should never serve as heating sources because they can create serious safety hazards.

Residents should continue monitoring weather alerts throughout the storm. Once conditions improve, homeowners can check for damage and begin clearing snow and ice from walkways and driveways.

Don’t Let a Winter Storm Take You by Surprise” Federal Emergency Management Agency, “Be Prepared for a Winter Storm”

#7811. Plaintiffs Contesting Tren de Aragua Membership Claims / Alien Enemies Act Application Still Can't Sue Pseudonymously

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Judge James Wesley Hendrix (N.D. Tex.) Friday in W.M.M. v. Trump (for more on the earlier Fifth Circuit en banc decision, see here):

On March 14, 2025, the President invoked the Alien Enemies Act—a federal statute that permits the President to deport foreign nationals who are engaged in an "invasion or predatory incursion" against the United States—to detain and remove members of Tren de Aragua, a Venezuelan terrorist group that traffics drugs and engages in other criminal activity. The petitioners, on behalf of a proposed class of Venezuelan nationals detained under the President's Proclamation, brought a habeas action in this Court. The petitioners argue that (1) the Proclamation exceeds the President's authority under the Alien Enemies Act and (2) the detainees have not received sufficient notice to challenge their removal.

After trips to the Fifth Circuit and the U.S. Supreme Court, the matter is back before this Court…. [T]he petitioners seek leave for the proposed class representatives to proceed under pseudonyms. The Court denies that motion because the named petitioners have not substantiated their conclusory allegations with evidence that they will suffer harm if their identities are disclosed. The Fifth Circuit found the petitioners' allegations insufficient to support their request to use pseudonyms [though it] {denied the petitioners' motion "without prejudice to any future determination by the district court regarding whether to allow any new class representatives to proceed under pseudonyms"}, and the petitioners have not persuaded this Court to depart from the Fifth Circuit's sound analysis….

Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 10(a) "require[s] plaintiffs to disclose their names in the instrument they file to commence a lawsuit." "Public access to this information is more than a customary procedural formality; First Amendment guarantees are implicated when a court decides to restrict public scrutiny of judicial proceedings." … "Judicial records belong to the American people; they are public, not private, documents." … The Fifth Circuit thus recognizes a "strong presumption against party pseudonymity."

D.A.A., T.I.A., and E.A.A. "have not shown that disclosure of their names would require them to disclose information of the utmost intimacy." … The petitioners do not request pseudonymity because the disclosure of their identities would reveal intimate details about their religion, sexuality, or family life. Rather, the petitioners do not want to disclose their identities because they do not want to publicize their alleged connection to TdA, a terrorist organization. But the Fifth Circuit has never suggested that this kind of information counts as a "sensitive and highly personal" matter that warrants pseudonymity.

Further, the petitioners dispute their designation as members of TdA. In other words, the petitioners allege that this designation is false. Yet the Fifth Circuit has implied that pseudonymity is proper only when the sensitive information—concerning, for example, one's religious beliefs—is true. Because the petitioners' alleged connection with TdA is, in their view, not true—and because it is not the kind of information that justifies pseudonymity—this Stegall factor cuts against the petitioners.

The Fifth Circuit also rejected the petitioners' argument that courts "should treat 'immigration matters, like the ones here, that disclose personal information,' as intimate information warranting pseudonymity," because the petitioners failed to explain how revealing "immigration matters" would "'disclose [any] personal information,' let alone information that makes pseudonyms appropriate." The petitioners have not provided any additional support for this argument to justify a departure from the Fifth Circuit's conclusion.

Relatedly, the Fifth Circuit rejected the petitioners' argument that they should be allowed to proceed under pseudonyms because several petitioners are seeking asylum. Two petitioners—T.I.A. and E.A.A.—seek asylum. The petitioners cite 8 C.F.R. § 208.6(a), which provides that information contained in an application for asylum "shall not be disclosed without the written consent of the applicant." But disclosing the petitioners' names will reveal only the fact that they have applied for asylum, not any information contained in the petitioners' respective asylum applications. {The information in the petitioners' respective asylum applications would likely not come before this Court anyway because the Court "lacks jurisdiction to hear an application for asylum."} Further, the petitioners still have not "shown that Venezuela penalizes asylum seekers." …

[P]etitioners [also] argue that public disclosure of their identities would subject them to physical violence in Venezuela. The Fifth Circuit rejected this argument because the petitioners expressed "only 'generalized concerns' about potential retaliation, directed toward either them or their families, in Venezuela or other countries as a result of the U.S. government identifying them with TdA." In the Fifth Circuit's view, the petitioners failed to produce "'plausible predictions of possible future violence,' let alone evidence of 'express threats or incidents' to anyone, including them or their families, arising out of identification with TdA." The petitioners' "evidence-less, generalized fears" thus did not "overcome the presumption against pseudonymity."

The Fifth Circuit's sound conclusion follows from the principle that courts should "not usually allow parties to proceed anonymously based on generalized concerns." Indeed, the Fifth Circuit recognized that "[c]ourts generally allow pseudonymity if there is 'reasonable[]' 'fear[]' of 'retaliatory physical … harm to the requesting party or even more critically, to innocent non-parties,' which may be considered in light of 'the anonymous party's vulnerability to such retaliation.'" "Express threats of violence would likely qualify, as would specific past incidents of violence or vandalism." But the "[l]ack of such express threats or incidents—or at least lack of highly plausible predictions of possible future violence—will usually count against pseudonymity."

Seeking to surmount this hurdle, the petitioners have now provided "evidence not previously provided to the Fifth Circuit[] regarding risk of retaliation due to the government's designation" of the petitioners as members of TdA. In particular, the petitioners have provided an expert's declaration describing how TdA members face threats of physical violence from Venezuelan "paramilitary groups," "right-wing opposition leaders," and "[r]ival gangs." The expert's declaration also says that the Venezuelan government features TdA members—many of whom are detained at the Center for Terrorist Confinement (CECOT) in Tecoluca, El Salvador—in political propaganda and exposes them to political violence.

But this additional evidence still provides "only 'generalized concerns' about potential retaliation." Each petitioner asserts that he "faces serious danger" of "retaliation, coercion, extortion, threatened prosecution, and violence from [TdA]-associated groups, rival gangs, and others" in El Salvador or Venezuela. But the petitioners have identified neither "express threats or incidents" nor "highly plausible predictions of possible future violence" to support pseudonymity. And the expert's declaration suffers from the same flaw. It says that alleged members of TdA "sometimes" face physical threats from groups that oppose the Venezuelan government, and "may" face threats or attacks from rival gangs. The two-page declaration lists no "[e]xpress threats of violence" or "specific past incidents of violence or vandalism" to support its generalized assertions.

Further, while the expert's declaration suggests that the Venezuelan regime may use members of TdA detained at CECOT as "propaganda tools" and subject those detainees to "political violence," these suggestions are conclusory. The expert's declaration does not even connect (1) the potential disclosure of the petitioners' identities in this lawsuit with (2) the likelihood that the petitioners will be used as "propaganda tools" and accordingly face "political violence" in El Salvador or Venezuela. The declaration merely states that its conclusions are based on "the situation in Venezuela for the men sent by the United States to CECOT in March 2025." In this respect, the declaration suggests that the Venezuelan regime singled out these men—and "disclos[ed] personal details about them"—solely on account of their detention at CECOT. Whether the detainees' identities were disclosed in a lawsuit in the United States was of no matter.

In any event, the Court lacks sufficient evidence to support the inference that denying the petitioners' motion to proceed under pseudonyms will cause them to face threats or physical harm in the future. Thus, the petitioners have not persuaded this Court that its analysis of this issue should differ from the Fifth Circuit's, given the generalized, conclusory nature of the petitioners' allegations.

{The Court previously granted the original named petitioners' motion to proceed under pseudonyms, because of "the sensitive and personal information about their immigration status and histories in this case." But the Court did so in a summary order at the inception of this litigation on a rapid timeline. Considering the en banc Fifth Circuit's statement on this matter and the lack of compelling evidence to distinguish the petitioners' present arguments from the arguments that the Fifth Circuit found unpersuasive, the Court finds it appropriate to deny the petitioners' motion for leave to proceed under pseudonyms.}

#7810. Kim Kardashian aims to retake bar exam

Reality TV star Kim Kardashian speaks onstage during the 2020 Winter TCA Tour on Jan. 18, 2020, in Pasadena, California. (Photo by David Livingston/Getty Images)

Reality TV star Kim Kardashian still holds ambitions to become a lawyer and plans to retake the bar exam—someday.

Kardashian, who failed the California bar exam in 2025, said she is “always thinking about the bar” and is “still all in,” she told People on Monday. “I’m going to take my time and wait until the moment is right, when I have some free time to focus on it.”

Kardashian, who plays a lawyer on Hulu’s legal drama All’s Fair, was among the 7,362 candidates who completed the July 2025 administration of the California bar, according to the State Bar of California.

The state’s test is considered one of the most difficult in the country, and only 54.8% passed last year and 48.3% in July, according to the state bar.

Kardashian did not attend law school and does not have an undergraduate degree. She has followed the state’s alternative pathway that allows candidates to take the bar exam by learning the law through apprenticeship and study.

California is one of the few states that allow lawyers to become lawyers by “reading the law.”

#7809. Tool Trials: Putting Ridgid’s Cordless Crown Stapler To the Test

Is a cordless stapler a real upgrade, or just a nice-to-have? I put one to the test to find out.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Last spring, I was sitting at home with my family watching football on a Sunday when my wife caught me doing what I often do: scrolling Zillow. “What don’t you like about the house we’re in?” she asked. I told her that ever since I finished the basement, I’d missed having a shop space to work on projects.

Her answer: “Then build that garage you always wanted.”

Fast forward eight months, and my new garage is up. I’m insulating the main level and sheathing it with OSB before adding cabinets and shelving and moving on to the upstairs. It’s a big garage; we’re talking 30-plus rolls of insulation on the main level, so on a run to pick up the next half-dozen rolls, I wandered down the tool aisle and saw the Ridgid 18V Cordless 3/8-in. Crown Stapler staring back at me.

Beyond getting the garage insulation up faster, it looked like a tool I’d keep using on future wiring and upholstery projects, and the same goes for anyone re-screening a porch, recovering a chair seat, or tacking down low-voltage wire.

A cordless 3/8-in. crown stapler kit with a 2.0 Ah battery and charger, depth adjustment, an onboard wire and screen attachment, and a built-in LED light.

The Ridgid 18V Cordless 3/8-in. Crown Stapler is a 3-lb. battery-powered stapler that runs on Ridgid’s 18V battery platform. It features an integrated LED light, an onboard wire and screen attachment, a depth adjustment knob, and a belt hook.

It drives 3/8-in. crown (T50) staples from 1/4 to 9/16 in. long. Ridgid claims it can drive 105 staples per minute and up to 6,800 staples on a single charge of a 4.0 Ah battery.

One last note, and in full transparency, I’m a regular user of Ridgid tools myself: Ridgid offers a lifetime service agreement on its tools as long as you register them within 90 days of purchase.

My goal was to install a half-dozen rolls of insulation, then run wire to an outlet to try out the wire attachment. I wanted to see how easy the tool was to use, whether it jammed, and what I liked and didn’t like about it.

The short version: this tool is awesome. No jams, nothing wonky. It’s as simple as load, point, and pull the trigger. It took a little playing with the depth knob to get the staples seating at the right depth, but I had it figured out within a handful of staples.

I really like the wire attachment. I try to keep my wiring clean and neat, usually with zip ties and tie mounts. With this attachment, running the wire was simple, and the stapler did it much more neatly than I expected.

I was also pleasantly surprised by the onboard LED light. It has its own trigger, separate from the firing trigger, so I could turn it on only when I needed it.

It’s also easy on the battery. I put up six rolls of insulation during the test and a couple more off camera, and the indicator on the 2.0 Ah battery didn’t budge.

There were a couple of things I didn’t like, though they’re minor. First, Ridgid advertises dry-fire lockout on this stapler, which I took to mean it wouldn’t fire once the staples ran out. On mine, it still did. To be fair, it never marred the work surface, which Ridgid lists as one of the lockout’s benefits, so it may be doing part of its job. But it was annoying to pull the trigger and have nothing come out, and it made it easy to miss that I was out of staples.

Second, the depth drifted. After every 20 or 30 staples, I’d notice they were no longer seating at the depth I’d set and were starting to sit proud. I don’t know if that was due to denser 2x4s or inconsistencies between strips of staples, but it was something to keep an eye on. When I noticed it, I’d add a few clicks on the depth knob.

I really like this tool. If you’re only insulating a garage, it’s really nice to have, but not essential. You could get by with a standard stapler. That said, the LED light, the wire attachment, and the price, especially with the battery and charger included, make this a tool I know I’ll use more than I expected on future projects.

A cordless 3/8-in. crown stapler kit with a 2.0 Ah battery and charger, depth adjustment, an onboard wire and screen attachment, and a built-in LED light.

The tool alone retails at The Home Depot for $119, but for the last few months, there’s been a special buy that includes the tool, a charger, and a 2.0 Ah Ridgid battery for $104.

Ridgid is owned by Emerson Electric Co., which makes the red Ridgid plumbing and pipe tools directly. The orange Ridgid cordless power tools, including this stapler, are made by Techtronic Industries (TTI), the company behind Milwaukee and Ryobi, under a licensing agreement with Emerson.

No. Staple guns need staples that match the tool’s crown width, leg length, and wire gauge. The Ridgid 18V crown stapler takes 3/8-in. crown staples from 1/4 to 9/16 in. long, including standard T50 staples. Other staplers may use different types, like narrow-crown or other heavy-duty series, so check the tool or the manual before you buy.

#7808. 31 Vintage Christmas Ideas Worth Bringing Back This Year

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 9, 2026 2:14 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Festive feather trees, classic cocktails, and decorative popcorn garlands: Yesteryear’s Christmas revelers really knew how to embrace the holiday season. This year, add a festive touch of seasonal cheer to your home with these old-school traditions. These vintage Christmas decorations and comforting treats will impress any guest, and create lasting memories for years to come.

Christmas teas aren’t just for the British. This traditional activity, which came to America in the 1830s as part of the temperance movement, brought families together to converse while drinking a variety of teas at long communal tables. So, fire up the tea kettle, make some fancy finger sandwiches, and enjoy a warm mug of tea with your loved ones.

The first artificial Christmas tree, which was a feather tree, dates back to mid-19th-century Germany. The thin-branched trees became popular in America in the 1920s, when European immigrants carried their holiday traditions to their new homes. Add a feather tree to your holiday decor for a touch of whimsy and historical charm.

Best Choice’s 9-foot tree has over 2,000 branch tips, strong branches, and beautiful flocking. Read the review.

Classic cocktails have made a comeback in bars around the country. Learn how to make a few favorites so you’ll have something to keep yourself warm, and impress your guests, over the holidays. Good choices for winter include the hot toddy (made with a bracing spirit like brandy, rum, or whiskey mixed with honey, spices, and boiling water) and the Tom and Jerry (a concoction of eggnog, brandy, and rum). Pouring your potables into fancy cocktail glasses makes them even more festive.

Jell-O long ago lost its spot as the star of the dessert table, but we think it’s about time the jiggly treat made a comeback. Pull out one of your grandma’s old recipe books and have fun constructing your very own holiday Jell-O mold, sure to be a crowd-pleaser at the kids’ table this year.

When families in the 1950s and ’60s didn’t want to maintain real Christmas trees, they opted for aluminum versions instead. Nowadays, these shimmering trees can add a little sparkly elegance to your seasonal decor while giving a nod to a long-lost trend. National Tree Company’s red tinsel tree is fire resistant, 6 feet high and has a 20-inch base diameter.

Before people adorned their trees with lights and ornaments, they decorated them with homemade popcorn garlands. Strings of popped kernels were budget-friendly and simple to construct. This year, spend quality time with your kids, parents, or grandparents making your own vintage popcorn garland. Be sure to pop extra corn to munch on as you work!

In the past, people traditionally thanked their regular letter carriers by giving them a small Christmas gift. Though we don’t always have the chance to develop relationships with our letter carriers today, it’s still a nice idea to give them a token of appreciation around the holidays. Just remember that federal guidelines stipulate that postal employees can’t accept gifts worth more than $20.

Stockings overflow with chocolates and toys on Christmas morning, but in simpler times children were excited and grateful to find oranges in their stockings. Put an orange in your child’s stocking this year as a reminder of your family’s good fortune, and for a healthy dose of vitamin C.

Tinsel became popular in the United States in the 1950s as people sought a way to add shimmer to their Christmas trees without using Christmas lights, which were considered a fire hazard. Re-create this vintage trend and give your tree a shiny, icy look by draping strands of tinsel on the branches. (Skip this tradition if you have pets, because tinsel is a choking hazard for them.)

With roots in solstice celebrations of ancient times, caroling is one of the oldest holiday traditions in the world. Channel your jolly ancestors and spread holiday cheer by taking your family Christmas caroling this year. Don’t worry if your singing voice doesn’t rival Beyoncé’s—this tradition is more about having fun than showing off your vocal chops.

In the early 20th century, people relied on trains as a primary mode of transportation. It’s no wonder that toy versions of these all-important vehicles started appearing underneath Christmas trees during that time. Set up a track around your Christmas tree to take your holiday visitors back in time, or gift a toy train to young relatives.

With the convenience of Netflix and DVDs, it’s easy to forget that children used to have to wait all year for their favorite classic Christmas specials to air on TV, and how excited they’d get when that day finally rolled around. Re-create the joys of a less plugged-in era by looking up the air times of old favorites, such as “A Charlie Brown Christmas,” or “How the Grinch Stole Christmas,” then whipping up a fresh batch of hot chocolate for a cozy night with the family.

Find a spot on the mantel for the classic figurines your family collected growing up, like Pixie Elves, Byers’ Choice Christmas Carolers, or Snowbabies. While the Elf on the Shelf might be the more common character right now, these guys were the original ones keeping watch over the house before Santa arrived.

If you don’t already have a Christmas village collection, consider starting one this year. The tradition of collecting miniature structures can be traced all the way back to the 17th century, but the charming ceramic houses and stores you know and love kicked off in the 1970s. Today, it’s easy to search up online sites and forums where Christmas village enthusiasts share their tips and tricks for creating elaborate setups.

We sing about it every year, but have you ever actually had a roasted chestnut? On a weekend afternoon or cozy evening, try your hand at roasting chestnuts—a stovetop will work just as well as an open fire for this.

Everything old is new again, and that includes ceramic Christmas trees. This ’70s Christmas decoration has roared back into style. If you don’t have one collecting dust in the basement, you can find the 15-inch Best Choice Products pre-lit ceramic Christmas tree, 18-inch Mr. Christmas ceramic tree, and others like them online.

If you have ever been to or seen photos of Dyker Heights Christmas lights, then you’re familiar with blow mold Christmas decorations. The playful plastic figurines first popped up on the market in the 1930s. Although many folks today like Christmas inflatables, we believe there’s enough room on the lawn for both.

Over the top, but worth it: BZB Goods’ Santa Claus with sleigh is 12 feet long and illuminated with internal lights.

While there are plenty of modern holiday hits to enjoy, set a retro mood by putting together a playlist with tracks from the likes of Bing Crosby and Frank Sinatra. While music-streaming services like Spotify already have plenty of holiday playlists to choose from, you can also curate a selection that reminds you of Christmases past.

Snail mail is so retro! Virtual Christmas greetings get the job done, but they aren’t nearly as sentimental as old-fashioned handwritten cards. Crisp stationery and seasonal stamps never fail to spread holiday cheer. Buy a boxed card set, or take a picture with your kids (or pet!) and incorporate it into a personalized greeting for everyone on your mailing list.

While it’s convenient to pick up a freshly cut Christmas tree from a big-box store’s parking lot, the tradition doesn’t have quite the same sense of holiday magic as venturing into a snow-covered wood to choose the perfect type of Christmas tree for your home. Depending on where you live, there are likely Christmas tree farms in your area that allow you to choose and cut down your own Christmas tree.

In the Middle Ages, the Lord of Misrule was a figure who was appointed to take charge of planning the Christmas activities in royal courts and noble houses. But this tradition came with a twist: The “Lord” often planned holiday pranks and jests. Try out this historic practice in your home this holiday season by giving children turns being the Lord of Misrule for the day. Allow the “Lord” to decide which treats to eat after dinner, which holiday special to watch, or letting them arrange the Elf on the Shelf for the following day.

While today’s Christmas supper typically features turkey or ham as a main dish, goose was once the centerpiece of many holiday dinner tables. In fact, eating goose for Christmas is a tradition that dates back to ancient Greece. A goose may be tricky to track down, but it’s generally possible to order one in advance from a high-quality butcher.

Tiny warm white lights are most common nowadays—on the tree and outside—but why not decorate with some retro flair? The big, colorful light bulbs you remember from previous decades are now available ineco-friendly LED bulbs. The burst of color outlining your house will make your home stand out from everyone else’s on the block.

With 3-inch C9 LED bulbs, the indoor/outdoor C9 LED lights from Wintergreen 17-foot strings really dazzle when used to frame the roof,

Today, getting dressed up for Christmas dinner typically means showing up in pair of elastic-waist pants to accommodate second helpings of turkey. In photos of midcentury Christmases, however, you’ll likely see men in ties and women in chic dresses with nary a pair of sweatpants in sight. Update your holiday dress code this year to bring back some vintage holiday glamour.

Evoke a vintage Christmas vibe by watching some holiday classics this December. Introduce your family to some timeless black-and-white picks like Miracle on 34th Street, White Christmas, and It’s a Wonderful Life. If you’re already familiar with these classics, screen an underrated holiday flick like Christmas in Connecticut or I’ll Be Seeing You.

Christmas crackers first made an appearance in Victorian England and are still popular in the U.K., but aren’t common on American holiday tables. A cracker is a wrapped cardboard tube that makes a loud cracking sound when pulled at both ends. They typically contain paper crowns as well as a small trinket and a card containing a joke or a piece of trivia, all of which are great dinnertime icebreakers.

You’re probably familiar with the “12 Days of Christmas” tradition because of the popular yuletide carol, but it’s a tradition that has largely died out in North America. Christians traditionally celebrated from December 25 to January 5 or 6, and gave one another small gifts each day. Extend the holiday season in your home by keeping festivities alive until Twelfth Night and continue to enjoy Christmas treats and festive holiday movies.

Though in many ways Christmas has become commercialized, you can bring back the spirit of giving that the holiday season once held by lending a hand to your neighbors or community. Help an elderly neighbor hang Christmas lights, volunteer at a toy drive for underprivileged children, or spend a day working at a soup kitchen to spread holiday cheer to those who need it most.

The origin of bottle brush Christmas trees dates back to the 1940s when, as the story goes, Addis Housewares Company manufactured the trees on the same machines the company used to make toilet brushes. Addis never did confirm the truth of the tree’s manufacture, but we’ll never look at a toilet brush the same way again. Though vintage version of these faux-snow-covered trees are hard to come by, you can find reproductions at retailers like Target and Crate and Barrel.

#7807. Your Level Might Be the Wrong Size, and It Could Be Throwing Off Your Work

A short level works for some projects, but longer surfaces need a wider check. Learn how to pick the right size and use it accurately.

Levels come in many different shapes and sizes, and figuring out how long a level should be for a certain project isn’t always straightforward. Choosing the right size matters because a level that’s too short can miss uneven spots, while one that’s too long can be difficult to use in tight spaces.

Here’s how much of a surface a level should cover, which sizes work best, and when overhang is okay.

It depends on the project, but a longer level is usually better for checking bigger surfaces. A shorter one might show that the middle of a board is level without catching a problem closer to either end.

The level doesn’t have to stretch across the entire surface, though. A 24-inch level can work on a four-foot shelf, for example, as long as the installer checks several spots along its length. For longer surfaces, a smaller level can sit on a long, straight board to check a wider area. A laser level is another option, especially when lining up things across a room.

The way the level sits on the material matters, too. A little sawdust or dirt underneath can affect the reading, so both surfaces should be clean. The tool also needs to sit firmly without rocking.

There’s no set rule for how much of a surface a level needs to cover, but it should fit comfortably and have enough contact to stay steady.

Different sizes work better for different jobs:

“Use a 4-foot carpenter’s level for framing whenever you have room for its length,” according to The Home Depot. “Warps or waves in the boards can throw off a shorter carpenter’s level.”

Another common concern is whether the level can hang over the edge of whatever is being checked. Some overhang is fine, provided the tool has enough support to stay steady.

If it starts tipping or rocking, a shorter level will likely work better. The bubble doesn’t need to be directly above the material, either. It can still give an accurate reading even when that part of the tool hangs past the edge.

#7805. Judiciary efforts to create rules for AI stalling amid concerns

Judiciary efforts to create rules for artificial intelligence use in the courts have been stalled amid concerns over the feasibility of reaching consensus on how the issues should be handled. (Photo by imaginima/Getty Images)

Judiciary efforts to create rules for artificial intelligence use in the courts have been stalled amid concerns over the feasibility of reaching consensus on how the issues should be handled.

The Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules, which advises the Judicial Conference of the United States, has been developing rules for AI use for several years, but efforts have encountered setbacks and resistance, slowing down the possibility of any new policy.

Attorneys, scholars and judges have criticized proposed evidentiary rules, such as one involving how to handle AI deepfakes, according to a story by Law360.

“Bottom line: I’m not hopeful at this point,” Maura R. Grossman, a professor at the University of Waterloo in Canada whose research has shaped the AI proposals, told Law360.
