#7804. 13 Potted Plants You Can—and Should—Winter Indoors

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 9, 2026 5:31 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Plenty of gardeners place their houseplants outdoors for the summer and enjoy them indoors the rest of the year. So why not try a similar strategy, and save a little money while you’re at it, by bringing your favorite cold-tender plants inside when the temperature drops so they’ll be ready to grow again when spring and summer rolls around?

Before you bring your outdoor plants in for the winter, you’ll need to do a bit of preparation. Start by inspecting them for pests and treating, if necessary. Repot if a plant needs it, and cut down on (or eliminate) fertilizing. Some plants can simply be brought indoors as houseplants, others should be forced into dormancy for a few months of cool storage, and still others are best kept going by making rooted cuttings. The following are a few cold-tender plants that you can bring inside each winter and then continue to enjoy outside for many summers to come.

While some palm trees are hardy in the winters of the Deep South, most palms need help to survive winter temperatures, even only to 55 to 60 degrees Fahrenheit . It’s possible to cover and winterize some palms planted in the ground, but potted palms should come indoors (preferably to a bright, humid spot). Move palms to an indoor location that gets lots of light. Water them regularly to keep the soil moist until spring, and carry them back outdoors after nights warm back up to at least 50 or 60 degrees.

Leave cacti outdoors as late into the season as possible so that the combination of shorter days and cooler nights will stimulate a dormancy response. You’ll need to keep an eye on the thermometer and know the low-temperature threshold for your particular type of cactus. Some species may be able to withstand 20-degree temperatures, but others cannot. If unsure, move potted cacti indoors as soon as cold drops to about 45 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit.

Stop watering cacti 3 to 4 weeks before the move so the plants are dry, and check them carefully for pets like mealy bugs or mites. In general, cacti do best in a cool location with minimal water, as they go dormant. Transition them back outside in early spring, gradually introducing sunlight if the plants show any sign of burning.

Citrus trees can actively grow and flower in winter, and may also ripen fruit if they’re pollinated. Even without winter growth, it’s a good idea protect these plants during the chilly months. As the days get shorter, move potted citrus trees (typically, dwarf varieties of lime and lemon trees) to an interim space outdoors that gets some protection from the elements, like a porch with radiant heat, and cut back on watering.

Before the first frost, move the citrus tree into a brightly lit indoor room, ideally between 55 and 70 degrees Fahrenheit. Citrus plants are sensitive to the drying effects of air, so it’s best to position them away from heat vents and cold drafts. Provide supplemental humidity with a pebble tray or regular misting.

Move tropical hibiscus plants indoors when overnight temperatures reach the low 50s. Place them in a brightly lit room, and treat them like regular houseplants. Cut back on watering and fertilizing during these cooler months. Try to avoid heat vents and cold drafts, and put the plants on a pebble tray to boost the ambient humidity, if necessary. Prune tropical hibiscus three times during late fall and winter (October, December, and February) to maintain the plant’s shape.

Prune jasmine vines by at least 25 percent before bringing them in for winter, letting them adjust gradually by bringing them inside at night and slowly lengthening the time spent indoors. Some or all of the plant’s leaves will fall off, but new ones will grow again in time. Bring jasmine into a sunny room before frosty weather arrives, and keep it away from drying air vents and drafts. Use a pebble tray to boost humidity to about 30 percent.

Coleus plants are grown for their stunning foliage and adaptability to shade. The plants are annuals in most regions, though, since they do not like temperatures below 50 degrees Fahrenheit and cannot survive temperatures below freezing. Bring the potted plant indoors once nights hover near 50 degrees. Repot the plant if it is outgrowing its container.

Another option is to propagate coleus stems to use next spring. Cut a 6-inch healthy stem, remove low leaves, and dip the stem in a rooting hormone before planting it in a container with moist potting mix. Cover the container with a plastic bag for a few weeks and keep it in a warm and sunny spot; water regularly.

Aromatic rosemary is a favorite cooking herb for many fall and winter dishes. However, the plant does not always survive winters in USDA Zones 6 or lower. Start by planting a rosemary in a well-draining container. Bring potted rosemary indoors before the first freeze. Keep it in a cool location with fairly high humidity, but avoid overwatering; if its roots stay damp and cool, it can develop root rot.

Feel free to harvest from the plant, but never cut off more than about 20 percent of the foliage and avoid cutting into woody main stems. You also can propagate rosemary indoors at the end of the season with 4- to 6-inch cuttings from a stem with no flowers.

Elephant ears, or taro, is a tropical plant that can survive a light frost only; a true freeze will kill the tuber. Simply move potted elephant ears indoors to a cool bright location. For those grown in the ground, carefully dig up the elephant ear tuber when cool weather approaches and the foliage dies back (they won’t survive winter outdoors in USDA Zone 6 and lower). Cut stems down to about 4 to 6 inches, and gently wipe off excess dirt.

Place the tuber in a warm, dark location with good air circulation to dry out for a few days. Wrap the bulbs in paper or drop them in a paper bag and store them in a cool, dry, dark place. Check them periodically for rot (throw rotten ones away) and insect damage (treat with an insecticide). Beware that nearly all its parts are toxic to pets and people if ingested—we don’t recommend bringing it indoors if you have young children.

It is technically possible to bring Boston ferns indoors and overwinter them in their active state, but it gets very messy very quickly. Instead, let them rest. Put them in a cool, moderately light to dark location that will not freeze, like an unheated basement or garage.

Before bringing your fern inside, hose it down on a warm (60-degree Fahrenheit) day to spray away insects and loose leaves. Give it a light trim, and shake and ruffle the fronds to drop debris before carrying the plant to its indoor spot. Moisten dry soil as needed until spring. Don’t be alarmed if some leaves pale or drop.

Geranium is another plant that likes to sleep the winter away. Dig the plants out of the ground before the first freeze, and gently knock the soil off the roots. Allow the plants to dry in a cool, shady location for a couple of days. Place the plants upside down in a paper bag and close the top. Store them in a cool, dark location that stays between 55 and 60 degrees.

About 2 months before the last frost date, trim the stored geraniums and plant them in moist potting soil with two leaf nodes below the soil line. You also can propagate cuttings or bring potted geraniums indoors to a sunny window.

Thyme is a flavorful and aromatic perennial herb, but a tender one in regions 5 or lower. Plant culinary thyme in a container in spring, keeping it in a sunny, bright location with well-draining soil. Bring it indoors for winter before the first frost. If the herb’s roots are peeking though the bottom of the pot or it looks crowded, repot the thyme when you bring it in. It also can be divided easily.

Be sure to place the container near a sunny window with a western or southern exposure in a room that maintains a 60- to 70-degrees Fahrenheit temperature for most of the day. Prune or pinch off flowers to preserve the herb’s flavor. Water as needed, allowing the container dry out between watering. You can fertilize every week or two with a diluted solution of fish emulsion or liquid seaweed. Harvest sprigs as needed for winter dishes.

Although Musa basjoo, Musella lasiocarpa, and a few other banana trees are quite cold hardy, most will not tolerate extended freezing temperatures. Potted banana plants can be brought indoors to a bright, sunny room to spend the winter in a slowed active state. They can take up some space indoors, so you also can help them sleep through winter. As the weather cools, gradually reduce watering. Before the first frost, cut the plant to 6 inches in height and move it to a dark, cool location. Keep the soil just moist until the weather warms in the spring.

The stunning evergreen cordyline is hardy only in the warmest growing zones, but potted cordylines can be moved indoors when temperatures dip into the 60s. Place them in a spot with good ventilation and consistent indoor temperatures; avoid placing them near air vents or in drafty areas. Increase humidity around cordyline by situating it in a humid room or on a saucer filled with pebbles and water, and avoid fluoride-treated tap water. Although the plant does not require dormancy in winter, it does like a rest, so cut water some during fall and winter.

We’ll help you set up your first garden—whether that’s a few pots on your patio, a raised bed, or an in-ground plot out back—and select the right plants for your soil and region.

#7802. U. Colorado Regent-vs.-Regents Lawsuit, Cannabis, Race, and Legislative Immunity

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From James v. Rennison, decided Friday by Judge Philip Brimmer (D. Colo.), plaintiff's allegations:

Regent Wanda James is an elected member of the University of Colorado Board of Regents …. Regent James is the second Black woman to be elected to the Board and is the only Black regent currently on the Board. Regent James is also a prominent Black cannabis owner and was the first Black owner of a cannabis dispensary in the United States. Regent James has used her position on the Board to advocate for communities of color.

In late 2024 and early 2025, the Colorado School of Public Health ("CSPH") developed a public health campaign called Tea on THC. The Tea on THC campaign included use of the following image:

Regent James used her position as a regent and as a private citizen to criticize the Tea on THC campaign, asserting that it invoked racist stereotypes. After Regent James criticized the Tea on THC campaign, the CSPH issued a public statement stating that it regretted any distress caused by the imagery used in the campaign and that it acknowledged its responsibility to reflect cultural awareness and sensitivity. In addition to criticizing the Tea on THC campaign, Regent James spoke publicly about the lack of Black leadership within the University of Colorado….

Approximately a month after Regent James spoke out against the Tea on THC campaign and the lack of Black leadership within the University of Colorado, the Board retained two law firms to evaluate allegations against Regent James. The allegations involved Regent James's speech. On July 2, 2025, the Board met to consider censure and sanctions against Regent James. The Board claimed that Regent James was responsible for CSPH's budget being reduced by 50%, although the budget reduction occurred before Regent James spoke about the Tea on THC campaign. Moreover, on January 31, 2025, the Governor's Office communicated to the legislature that it was seeking full elimination of CSPH's cannabis-related funding. At the July 2, 2025 meeting, by a vote of seven-to-one, the Board voted to censure Regent James under Regent Policy 2.M, finding that she had violated Regent Policy 2.J.1 and Regent Policy 2.J.2, which respectively confer regents with a duty of care and duty of loyalty.

In addition to censuring Regent James, the Board adopted a sanctions resolution. The sanctions resolution removed Regent James from all regent committee assignments, precluded Regent James from any future regent committee assignments, and barred Regent James from attending internal or external University of Colorado events in her official capacity.

Regent James sued the other regents, alleging violation of the First Amendment and race discrimination, but the court held that their actions were protected by absolute legislative immunity:

"The principle that legislators are absolutely immune from liability for their legislative activities has long been recognized in Anglo–American law." … Legislative immunity is "similar in origin and rationale to that accorded Congressmen under the Speech or Debate Clause." …

"Absolute legislative immunity attaches to all actions taken in the sphere of legitimate legislative activity." … Courts have found that board members of educational districts and facilities are entitled to legislative immunity, provided that they are acting in a legislative capacity.

Certain duties of the regents appear to be done in a legislative capacity. Traditionally, legislators have "[t]he authority to pass laws and the power of the purse." The Board of Regents "enact[s] laws for the government of the university," and has "control and direction of all funds of and appropriations to the university." Furthermore, the regents must be elected. Thus, the regents bear similarities to legislators in traditional legislative bodies, such as state legislatures….

"[C]ourts have repeatedly recognized that a legislature voting to censure or discipline one of its own members is a core legislative act," thus falling within … the functional test of legislative immunity…. Defendants sanctioned Regent James for violating the duty of care and duty of loyalty. The sanctions resolution indicates that this was due to, among other things, allegations that Regent James requested that officials in the executive and legislative branches pull funding from the Colorado School of Public Health and shift funding from the Tea on THC campaign to grants for marijuana business owners. If the regents were unable to enforce the Board's internal policies, the adoption of such policies would be meaningless, and the regents would be hindered exercising their duties. For example, the regent's statutory power over the "control and direction of all funds of and appropriations to the university," would be diminished if regents could not enforce internal policies prohibiting a regent from acting contrary to the financial interests of the University of Colorado.

{Legislative immunity does not turn "on the official's motive or intent," so it is irrelevant to the immunity analysis whether defendants actually censured and sanctioned Regent James due to violations of the duties of loyalty and/or care or if that was a pretext to censure and sanction Regent James for discriminatory reasons.} …

Frederick Richard Yarger, Meghan Frei Berglind, and William Daniel Hauptman (Wheeler Trigg O'Donnell LLP) represent defendants.

Get the SmartJacket water heater blanket at Amazon or Walmart.

Buying a large kit to insulate a small tank can be a waste of money, so it’s more cost-effective to buy only the material you need. Reflecto-Foil’s water heater jacket is designed to work with water heater tanks up to 40 gallons to save cash and avoid wasted material.

This kit features a roll of Class 1/Class A fire-rated foil insulation, foil tape, and the spacers (small chunks of foam used to make a consistent circumference around the tank) necessary for a good fit. The roll of insulation measures 76 inches long by 48 inches wide to cover most smaller water heater tanks with ease. And because it’s fiberglass-free, there’s no need to worry about wearing long sleeves or other protective gear.

Get the Reflecto-Foil 40-gallon water heater blanket at Amazon.

In choosing the best water heater blankets among those currently on the market, we looked at two top factors: material and size. Our list of recommendations covers the most popular types of water heater blanks, including thick fiberglass options as well as thinner foam and foil options.

We also made sure to include a range of sizes on our list with options to cover most water heater shapes. For oddly shaped water heaters with awkward piping, we included recommendations for several easy-to-cut options that can fit snugly around even the most difficult water heater shapes or those in tight spaces.

Before shopping for a water heater blanket, read this section to understand the factors and features to keep in mind. This will help you make an informed decision.

When perusing water heater blankets, you’ll notice that there are a few different types available. This mostly comes down to the type of insulating material. Some are easier to work with during installation than others, as they often need to be trimmed to fit individual water heaters.

You may also find combinations of materials, such as fiberglass insulation with a foil face. This can offer the best of both worlds, as it uses a thick, insulating layer of air pockets and radiates heat back into the tank.

Water heaters, like most appliances, come in different sizes. The size of house and family and the number of sinks and showers all affect how large a water heater a home needs. While water heaters range between 30 and 98 gallons, 40-, 50-, and 60-gallon tanks are the common sizes used in homes.

Water heater blankets also come in similar sizes, so it’s important to find one that will work for your tank. If you have a 50-gallon tank, finding a water heater blanket to fit it should be no problem. Water heater blankets large enough to fit 98-gallon tanks, commonly found in commercial settings, may be harder to track down.

When it comes to materials such as fiberglass, cotton, and denim, the thicker the water heater blanket, the better it will be at insulating. A water heater located in a cool basement calls for a thicker blanket. Thicker blankets will do a better job of separating the cool air and the heat radiating from the tank than thinner ones.

Because foil works primarily by reflecting the heat instead of relying on an air-pocket barrier, it needn’t be thick to function efficiently. Most water heater blankets made with foil are less than ½ inch thick, which is another reason foil water heater blankets are so easy to work with.

Just like your home’s insulation, water heater blankets come in a variety of insulation ratings. These ratings are described as R-value, where the R stands for resistance. The higher the R-value, the more resistance the insulation has against heat transfer. Essentially, more is better.

The highest R-value you’re likely to find for a residential water heater blanket is R-11, but values of R-7 and R-8 are more common. To get the most from your investment, it’s best to use the water heater blanket with the highest R-value.

It’s important to keep in mind, though, that foil-type insulation rarely offers an R-value; R-values apply to fiberglass and other similar types of insulation.

Water heaters have burner assemblies that get very hot. The point of insulating a water heater is to save energy and money, not cause a fire. Different water heater blanket materials have varying degrees of fire resistance to combat that risk. While the most common designation is Class 1/Class A, it’s helpful to know which types are the most fire resistant.

If fire resistance is of utmost importance, a fiberglass or foil water heater blanket is the way to go. Some fiberglass or foil products aren’t fire rated, but that doesn’t mean they’re unsafe. Just be sure to keep the insulation clear of the burner by a few inches.

There are two types of water heaters: electric and gas. Electric water heaters have a heating element inside that energizes and heats the water that surrounds it. Gas water heaters have burners underneath that kick on to heat water through convection.

Fortunately, water heater blankets are interchangeable between the two water heater types. However, if you have a gas-powered heater, it’s crucial that the blanket doesn’t cover or otherwise obstruct the flue (aka exhaust) at the top. If you have an electric model, the blanket must not cover or obstruct its control box or access panel, typically located on the side of the tank. Also, be sure to cut the insulation back from the burner by at least 2 inches while installing.

For additional information about buying and using the best water heater blanket, consider the answers to these frequently asked questions.

A great water heater blanket will offer a blend of insulation value, cost-effectiveness, and fire resistance.

It depends on the size of your tank. Generally speaking, manufacturers label their water heater blankets according to the size of the tank they’ll cover. If you’re unsure, measure your tank’s height and circumference, and compare it to the measurements on the package.

Water heater blankets are low maintenance, but fiberglass, cotton, and denim can begin to smell and stop insulating if they get wet. It’s a good idea to check on your water heater blanket a few times a year to ensure it’s still in good condition.

Undamaged water heater blankets may far outlast a water heater. The average gas water heater lasts between 8 and 12 years, while the average electric water heater lasts 10 to 15 years. A water heater blanket kept in good condition will outlast a water heater without issue.

The most efficient way to install a water heater blanket is to measure the height and circumference of your tank before unrolling the product, allowing for an extra 2 inches for the circumference so you can overlap the product. Premeasuring allows you to swiftly cut the product to size using cutter or scissors. Wrap the tank with the blanket, and secure it in place with foil tape placed vertically along the seam. Cover the top of the tank with two half circles of material, and secure it in place with foil tape. Ensure that you cut openings for the venting hood, pressure relief valve, burner access cover, and wiring connection box. Make the holes about 2 inches larger than each opening to allow airflow.

Yes. Any steps you can take to keep your water hot without additional reheating of the water is worth it. The water heater blanket does just this and is an inexpensive purchase. In most cases, you should be able to recoup your investment when installing an insulator blanket.

Yes. When properly installed, hot water heater blankets are safe to use. The most important thing is to ensure proper airflow around all fixtures by cutting slightly larger openings around valves, hoods, burners, etc. Don’t forget that some blankets contain fiberglass, and those installing the product should wear safety goggles, a dust mask, gloves, and long sleeves, then carefully clean the area after installation to remove any stray fiberglass fibers.

#7800. I Thought Multi-Tools Were a Gimmick — Then I Took One on a Camping Trip

If, like me, you think multi-tools are gimmicky gadgets, you might change your mind once you discover how handy they are when your toolbox isn’t within reach.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

I admit I scoffed when my partner first started raving about his Leatherman Wave+ multi-tool. I thought it looked like an expensive, over-elaborate gadget that was destined to gather dust in a junk drawer.

However, as a keen hiker and camper, I’ve discovered how useful it is to have pliers, knives, a saw, scissors, files and other tools packed into one compact, quality piece of kit. I’ve also watched my tech-obsessed partner regularly reach for its precision tools when tinkering with his electrical equipment.

Ahead, I’ll share how a tool I once dismissed as a gimmick earned a permanent spot in my pack, and what two experts think makes a Leatherman worth the price tag.

I had to realize that our Leatherman Wave+ isn’t meant to replace a well-stocked toolbox to understand its value. Instead, it fills the gap when dedicated tools aren’t conveniently available or really needed.

At home, I regularly use the tool’s tiny scissors to carefully prune dead leaves from our many houseplants, the knife to open packages and the small screwdriver to tighten the legs on my glasses. My partner is an IT professional who also has an impressive collection of synthesizers, and he regularly reaches for the tool to make small technical repairs and splice wires.

I’ve found the Wave+ even more useful when we’re borrowing my parents’ campervan, hiking, or camping. The bottle opener is handy for those after-adventure beers, the serrated knife slices baguettes for trailside sandwiches, the saw cuts small, dry branches for kindling, and the screwdriver has adjusted our portable stove and tightened folding chairs.

The pocket-sized multi-tool packs 18 functions into a stainless-steel form that measures just four inches when closed and weighs 8.5 ounces. Alongside the tools I’ve mentioned, it has pliers, bit drivers, a wire stripper and crimper, a ruler, an extra knife blade and file, and an admittedly slightly-tricky-to-use can opener.

While I don’t regularly use all 18 tools, and I might never use some, having the selection provides peace of mind, especially in remote places.

Daniel Kilburn, founder of Emergency Action Planning and a preparedness expert, has carried his Leatherman Surge since his military service in 2006. “It’s an expedient tool to have on hand when you know you’re going to be someplace where you won’t have access to any others,” he says.

Scott Emanuel of knives, multi-tools, and outdoor equipment retailer Heinnie Haynes is also a multi-tool convert. He appreciated having one for quick fixes while renovating his cottage, and particularly rates the needle-nose pliers, which rival standard models rather than acting as an emergency substitute.

Kilburn suggests multi-tools can be a useful starting point for someone who doesn’t own a toolbox, and at the other end of the spectrum are the tinkerers and prepared problem-solvers Emanuel sees as natural fits.

“The person who will value a Leatherman is the one who spends their after-hours in the garage building stuff that they probably never need, it’s the kind of self-reliant and prepared person who you rely on to solve a problem,” Emanuel says.

The Leatherman Wave+ currently costs $129.95, meaning it should be a well-considered purchase rather than an impulse buy.

It’s reassuring to know that you’ll be investing in a refined product designed because of a genuine practical need. Founder Tim Leatherman conceived a pliers-based multi-tool after encountering car and plumbing problems while traveling through Europe in the 1970s, and after careful development, he launched the original Pocket Survival Tool in 1983.

Today you’re paying for that established reputation and durable construction, and Leatherman backs its products with a 25-year warranty.

“They’re ridiculously well built, really well regarded, and their choice of tools is good,” Emanuel says. He describes sought-after Leathermans as the “collectible top end of the multi-tool market.”

Kilburn recalls seeing lower-priced multi-tools failing his comrades during their military career. “Some disintegrate over time because they were just cheaply made with poor-quality material [and] poor-quality steel,” he says. His Leatherman Surge, meanwhile, has lasted over 20 years. If replacing it again, he says he would choose Leatherman over his backup Gerber multi-tool because he prefers its feel and durability.

Leatherman makes a wide range of multi-tools, so it pays to consider which functions you’ll genuinely use. The Signal model adds outdoor-focused features suited to camping, including a ferrocerium rod, emergency whistle and sharpener, but omits scissors. I use scissors enough for plant pruning, first aid and gear repairs that the Wave+ remains the better fit for me.

If you’re unlikely to use most of its functions, a smaller, cheaper multi-tool could make more sense. The Wave+ is also heavier than minimalist models, and there’s a learning curve when figuring out where everything lives.

Don’t forget that a premium multi-tool only represents good value if you look after it. We remove dirt after outdoor adventures and dry and lubricate it before storing. We also avoid forcing it to tackle jobs better suited to full-size tools. I wouldn’t, for example, choose its compact saw over a dedicated full-size version for pruning substantial tree branches in my yard.

If you’re using a Wave+ in the UK, like me, be aware of the country’s knife laws. You need a “good reason” to carry it in public because its blades lock. However, Emanuel explains that the legal language is ambiguous, so you shouldn’t assume you can carry one wherever you go just because it’s part of a multi-tool.

The Wave+ has convinced me that a good multi-tool is more than merely an expensive gimmick. It may not replace dedicated tools, but having so many functions at my fingertips in a form that is so compact, portable and easy to use makes it a practical, worthwhile investment.

The Wave Plus is a multi-tool workhorse. It packs 18 tools in one, including sharp blades, spring scissors, wire cutters, and more.

#7798. 8 Reasons a Contractor Might Give You an Outrageously High Estimate

If you just got a quote for a home repair that made your eyes water, there's probably a reason it's so high. A team of contractors weighs in with possible explanations.

If you just got a quote from a contractor that was way more than you thought it would be, join the club…it happens to the best of us. In fact, it’s a pretty common occurrence. Sometimes, though, the quote is so high that you can feel your mouth forming words you shouldn’t be saying. As someone who has been on both sides of such interactions, I can say that contractors don’t like them any more than you do. They know you can shop around, and they need your business. So what’s the deal with ridiculously high quotes?

I didn’t find any shortage of contractors willing to weigh in on this topic — one that is near and dear to their professional hearts. If a quote just made you hyperventilate, take a deep breath and check out some of the possible reasons why it’s so much higher than you expected.

“If an HVAC unit has a defective part that needs replacement, most of my clients will immediately ask how much the replacement part costs,” says HVAC technician Tamer Sayed. “I always tell the current market price and the misunderstanding often starts here. A few clients forget to take into account the labor and consultation fees. They assume they only had to pay for the replacement part.”

The same thing can happen with plumbing and electrical jobs. The part needed to get things working again may be small and inexpensive, and it may only account for a small portion of the quote. Sometimes the labor quote seems excessive, and that’s usually because the client doesn’t understand what’s involved with the repair.

Jake Vincett, a builder from the UK, makes this observation: “A lot of the time, the customer is comparing quotes for different work, because the cheaper one has included a surface repair whereas the more expensive one has quoted for fixing the underlying problem…It’s common that the customer doesn’t know or consider the amount of work going into a project. A new driveway isn’t just laying tarmac – it’s digging out the old one, laying the sub base, etc.”

Plumbing, electrical and HVAC expert Bob Cardwell adds: “It’s often not only one problem to fix but a bunch of small fixes. Even though it might be possible to fix the original problem without addressing the additional issues, an experienced and reliable technician will not ignore them, will try to fix them and will discuss them with the homeowner.”

Failing to provide a quote that addresses underlying issues and then delivering a sky-high bill at the end doesn’t just make the customer unhappy, says HVAC and plumbing expert Ryan Osterkamp. “It can make them feel like we don’t know what we’re doing.”

Osterkamp is used to hearing customers say: “I can go get that part for $X at Home Depot.” What they aren’t thinking about is the amount of training and expertise that made it possible for our technician to quickly and accurately diagnose the issue, have the supplies they need in their truck and be able to do the repair same day. Sure, you may save money by going with the guy on Facebook that works out of an old, unlabeled truck, but if his work doesn’t hold up, will he fix it without giving you the runaround? Is he insured? Does he offer a warranty?”

Tariffs, inflation and the economy in general are pushing prices up, and the dollar has lost a lot of its purchasing power for the average American. The same is true for contractors. “The fact of the matter is, we’re working harder now and making less,” says remodeling contractor Kevin Cullen. “In today’s economy, a lot of people are chasing the price to the bottom and shopping for the cheapest number. Unfortunately, they usually get what they pay for.”

A contractor who knows problems might creep up, such as a rotten subfloor that needs replacement during a toilet repair, makes an effort to warn customers as part of the quote. Potential problems aren’t always obvious. “There are times,” says Nika Tveretinova, who operates an HVAC business in Sacramento, “when the actual fix isn’t that complicated, but it’s the access that makes things tough—especially with equipment installed in an attic or cramped quarters. Sometimes we also find an old installation that needs a safety or code correction before we can put everything back together.”

In such situations, a higher-than-expected quote that you can reject is far better than a higher-than-expected bill you have to pay because the work is already completed.

Joshua Kurz founded NumeralQ, a home improvement pricing guide, and he cautions against comparing a bid you receive from a contractor to information you find online. “Owners often find an estimate online, and rather than waiting for a bid, they assume that number will be the actual cost. These estimates are helpful when determining a budget, but they are not interchangeable for actual bids. A 1,500 sq ft roof in one market will not necessarily cost the same in another market, and bids can even differ for neighboring houses.”

If you find a guy on Facebook who charges a low price to do a repair, there’s no guarantee that the repair will last or be up to code. When that person makes a mistake, a licensed contractor working on the same system at a later date might have to fix it, especially when inspectors are involved.

“Over a 40-year career,” says Cullen, “I’ve found many surprises: unsupported headers, no king or jack studs, undersized headers, poorly installed headers that aren’t flush and have gaps, termite damage, carpenter ant damage, water damage, mold. That’s not every job, but you never know when a homeowner bought a house in which a Rube Goldberg did the work on it.”

Sometimes a house is in such poor condition that a small repair, such as stopping a plumbing leak, can turn into a major project that involves replacing pipes, walls or subfloors. Rather than simply declining the repair, some contractors will offer a ridiculously high quote to avoid falling into a sinkhole of extra work. If the customer accepts the quote, the contractor won’t lose money by taking the job. A customer who rejects a bid can keep shopping with no harm done.

It supplied enough juice to jump all three dead batteries and took less than three hours to recharge. The compressor feature inflated our bike, car, and truck tires, but it took nearly 30 minutes to completely fill the truck tire. Still, the JackPak isn’t meant as a replacement for a commercial tire inflator, but it will get the job done when a service station isn’t nearby.

We liked the bright LED light on the JackPak, and it doubles as a powerbank for charging devices. It also features a low-power sleep mode that keeps its internal battery from discharging for up to 36 months.

Get the JackPack jump starter with air compressor at Lowe’s or The Home Depot.

When a battery goes dead and a car is stuck in a parking lot or across town (or the side of the road), there’s a lot on the line. We know that, so we tested the jump starters with air compressors on our own depleted car and truck batteries and to inflate a range of tires.

We tested each product by jumping a dead car, truck, and riding mower batteries. We also used a multimeter to determine the voltage from the jump starters. We tested the jump starters over a 2-week period, connecting each one to the various battery terminals and then attempting to start the vehicle.

We also drained some of the air from bike, car, and truck tires to test the built-in compressors. For the inflation tests, we partially deflated bike, car, and truck tires and then timed how long it took each inflator to return the tires to the recommended pressure. During these inflation tests, we paid close attention to how easily the air chucks connected to the valve stems, whether they created a secure seal, and how well they held up through repeated use. We also considered whether the compressors operated consistently under pressure or showed signs of strain, as well as how intuitive and responsive the controls were throughout the process.

We awarded points based on a rubric: the better a jump starter/inflator did on a test or assessment, the higher the points. The products that excelled were given awards based on their strengths, while those that failed were removed from our lineup.

Carrying a jump starter with an air compressor means drivers can handle emergencies and repairs without calling for help (or when help isn’t available). And who doesn’t enjoy a little self-reliance? These devices include built-in jumper cables to clamp onto the positive and negative terminals of a dead battery. It sounds straightforward, but shopping for one of these devices requires a bit of background and know-how. The following sections will break down the most important considerations to keep in mind while shopping for a battery jumper with air compressor.

Jump starters equipped with air compressors include one of two battery types: lithium-ion and lead-acid.

The best jump starters with air compressors—and all portable jump starters, for that matter—have an onboard battery that provides ample power to start a vehicle or operate the compressor. In most cases, the battery size of these portable chargers is described in milliampere hours (mAh) or amp hours (Ah)—1,000mAh equals 1Ah.

Higher mAh or Ah ratings equals a larger capacity to store power, so higher ratings mean more batteries charged and tires inflated between recharges. Generally speaking, most portable jump starters use batteries between 10,000 and 35,000mAh. Remember that higher capacity batteries are heavy, and get heavier as the storage increases.

The purpose of a jump starter is to provide a vehicle with enough power to turn over and fire up the engine, then allow the vehicle’s alternator to continue charging the battery. The amount of power a jump starter needs to accomplish this task is determined by the engine.

Small gasoline engines, such as four-cylinder engines found in most cars (and progressively larger vehicles) don’t require much power. But larger eight-cylinder engines require a bit more. And, because of the extremely high compression ratios of diesel engines, large models found in heavy-duty pickups, RVs, and power equipment require even more power. In general, 1,000A or more will do the trick.

Many manufacturers today don’t explicitly list the amount of power provided by their chargers. Instead, they discuss the types of engines their chargers can handle. This is only a concern for diesel vehicles, as any jump starter will handle most gasoline engines.

While it might seem that jumper cables are all created equal, modern jump starters offer additional safety features. Today’s models protect a vehicle’s electrical system and the person using the cables from sparking or reverse polarity, which happens when the user connects the clamps to the wrong terminals—something that’s very easy to do in the dark. Reverse polarity can wreak havoc on the sensitive electronics in today’s vehicles, so this is a crucial feature.

These units will detect the reverse polarity or contact between the clamps and prevent the unit from expelling stored energy through them. Often, a small light or audible alarm will alert the user so you can understand what’s occurring and why the jump starter isn’t charging the vehicle.

When choosing the best jump starter with an air compressor, there is some variance in the amount of pounds per square inch (PSI) offered by these models. Most models produce around 100 PSI—more than enough for any road vehicle’s tires. Most vehicle tires require just 30 to 40 PSI.

Some models offer 150 PSI or more, which is as much pressure as a traditional home air compressor. Are they necessary for typical vehicle repairs? No. But it might take these compressors less time to boost up a tire on the side of the road, so they could be worth the consideration and splurge.

Several additional features might make a portable jump starter with an air compressor a bit more attractive to consumers.

Even with all of this background on choosing the best jump starter with air compressor, you might have questions. The following section is a collection of some of the most frequently asked questions about battery jump starters with air compressors, so be sure to check for an answer to your question below.stions about jump starters with air compressors, so be sure to check for an answer to your question below.

This depends on the vehicle, with smaller engines requiring just a few hundred amps and larger engines requiring 1,000 or more amps. Consider erring on the side of caution and choosing a car battery jump starter from this guide, as they all boast at least 1,000A.

Many units include their own AC adapters for charging via an outlet in a home garage. Others might have plugs to attach a standard extension cord for charging. Some also feature 12V ports for charging in a vehicle.

Most manufacturers suggest charging a jump starter with an air compressor every 30 days to ensure it’s in good working order.

Let your vehicle run for 15 to 30 minutes to allow the battery to recharge.

You can expect to get 3 to 5 years of service, depending on quality and usage.

#7796. Lawyers’ AI use doesn’t justify slashing $115K fee award, appellate court says

A federal appeals court has rejected an argument that a law firm’s use of artificial intelligence should shrink its fee award. (Image from Shutterstock)

A federal appeals court has rejected an argument that a law firm’s use of artificial intelligence should shrink its fee award.

Reuters reported Monday that the 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Denver upheld a $115,000 fee awarded to defense lawyers at Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck by the lower court in a trade secrets dispute. The trial court had ruled that the fee was reasonable.

“Plaintiffs have not shown that defense counsel’s use of AI rendered the hours that ​they actually expended unreasonable,” wrote 10th Circuit Judge Carolyn McHugh for a unanimous three-judge panel.

The appeals court also upheld the ​dismissal of the lawsuit.

In her opinion, McHugh acknowledged that AI and similar research tools can make attorneys more efficient. But she stressed that lawyers must still verify legal authorities and arguments themselves.

According to Reuters, the case began in 2024, when industrial motor-efficiency equipment maker Flux Drive filed a suit against a Chinese manufacturer, alleging that one of its former engineers had stolen proprietary information and given it to them. After the case was dismissed, Flux Drive was ordered to pay the defendants’ legal fees. On appeal, the company argued that the defense billed for “ministerial tasks,” and that AI use should have lowered the bill.

The defendants countered that their lawyers checked every piece of AI-assisted research, and that Flux Drive pointed to no specific inflated entry, redundant task or unreasonable charge.

Brownstein Hyatt partner Christopher Ottele, who represented the defendants, called AI a powerful tool that sophisticated firms should embrace.

“This ​decision confirms that the use of AI is not a substitute for the judgment and analysis that attorneys still ​must exercise in every filing with the court,” Ottele told Reuters.

Counsel for the plaintiffs did not immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comment.

#7795. Deference, the Insurrection Act, and Statutory History

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

I recently wrote about the Ninth Circuit's decision in Newsom v. Trump, which ruled that Trump's federalization of the California National Guard last year, was illegal. Previously I assessed the Supreme Court's ruling in the closely related case of Trump v. Illinois. Today, we have a guest post on these and related issues, by Professor Joshua Braver of the University of Wisconsin. Josh is one of the nation's leading experts on the law regulating domestic use of the armed forces, and my coauthor on two articles about exclusionary zoning (see here and here).

The Volokh Conspiracy and I are pleased to be able to feature his post on this extraordinarily important issue. It is cross-posted with the Just Security site. What follows below is written by Josh Braver, not me (Ilya Somin):

On October 23, in Newsom v. Trump, the Ninth Circuit struck down President Donald Trump's June 2025 federalization of the National Guard in Los Angeles. Although I agree with the result, I disagree with its reasoning on deference. The issue is whether courts should defer to the president, that is, give a president significant leeway in their assessment of the facts on the ground and whether those facts meet the statutory criteria for deploying the military. The Ninth Circuit decided to be, in its words, "highly deferential" in both its decision on Los Angeles and its decision on federalizing the Guard in Portland. That line of reasoning also influenced the Seventh Circuit's decision to give "great deference" in the Chicago case.

In adopting this "highly deferential" standard, the Ninth Circuit claimed to rely on the statutory history of domestic military deployment. But that history actually cuts in the opposite direction, against deference, as I discuss extensively in an article just published in the Emory Law Journal. The significance of that history extends beyond the recent decision in Newsom, which concerned the novel use of a little-known statute, 10 U.S.C. § 12406. The larger question is whether courts should defer to a president when they invoke the Insurrection Act, the main and most fearsome statute for domestic deployment of the military.

Legal commentators had previously recognized these stakes in the last significant decision on these domestic deployments. After the Supreme Court blocked the deployment of the Guard in Chicago last December, some called the decision a "pyrrhic victory;" as Jack Goldsmith put it, the Insurrection Act still "lie[s] in the wings." In Goldsmith's view, the Insurrection Act is "much more robust" than § 12406, and the "power authorized here is astounding," in large part because of the "greater claim to presidential deference" under the Insurrection Act. According to Goldsmith and co-author Bob Bauer, "The president will receive very significant deference from courts in his determination that an Insurrection Act predicate is satisfied." The Ninth Circuit's decision on deference only adds fuel to that blazing fire of deference for the Insurrection Act. That line of reasoning is, however, not well supported by the statutory history of the Insurrection Act.

One of Congress's powers under Article I, Section 8 is to provide for "calling forth" the militia for domestic deployment. The most famous, broadest, and most well-used example of Congress exercising this power is the much-discussed Insurrection Act. But the 2025 deployments in Los Angeles, Portland, and Chicago concerned a heretofore obscure statute, 10 U.S.C. § 12406, which permits federalization of the National Guard in cases of (a) invasion, (b) rebellion, or (c) the president's inability, with the regular forces, to execute the laws of the United States. Newsom v. Trump dealt with the rebellion prong (which Ilya Somin discussed here), while the Supreme Court in Trump v. Illinois addressed the prong involving inability to execute the laws with regular forces.

But there is a specific question of deference. The baseline in statutory interpretation is no deference. Legislatures pass laws and then courts interpret them. When the executive exceeds a statute's authorization as interpreted by the judiciary, courts rule that the action is unlawful. That baseline can be displaced for various reasons. But the most straightforward reason is when the statutory text itself provides for deference, and this was the Ninth Circuit's focus.

Statutes may confer discretion on the president by using subjective terms, such as when a provision turns on what the president "judges," "considers," "deems," "determines," or "finds." For example, in Trump v. Hawaii, the Supreme Court concluded that the statute "exudes deference to the President" because the Immigration and Nationality Act, by its terms, authorizes the president to suspend the entry of aliens whenever he "finds" that their entry would be detrimental to the interests of the United States.  As elaborated in my Emory Law Journal article, the text of the Insurrection Act confers deference in only one of the four conditions for its use, because it sometimes uses the term "considers" and sometimes does not.

In contrast,  there are no subjective discretion-conferring terms in 10 U.S.C. § 12406 that could be construed to confer deference on the president. Both in its recent opinion and in its earlier stay order, the Ninth Circuit acknowledged as much:

"Section 12406 does not include express language making the President the sole judge of whether a required exigency exists. Consequently, if we were considering the text of § 12406 alone, we might conclude that the President's exigency determination is subject to review like certain other factual findings that are preconditions for executive action under a statute."

Nonetheless, the court still decided to be "highly deferential" for two reasons:

"[T]he history of Congress's statutory delegations of its calling forth power and a line of cases interpreting those delegations, beginning with Martin [v. Mott], strongly suggest that our review of the President's determinations in this context is especially deferential."

For the moment, let's leave the court's reliance on Mott to the side, though I will return to it later in the essay. What concerns me here is the Circuit's ostensible reliance on the "history of Congress's statutory delegations." That history, the Ninth Circuit acknowledged, consists largely of the evolution of the Insurrection Act, the principal statute governing domestic military deployments, and the one from which 10 U.S.C. § 12406 descends. For the statutory history of domestic deployments, the court relies solely on the Insurrection Act, but it does not examine that history in much depth. The question is whether those changes in text of the statute over time support deference. They do not.

Statutory History of the Insurrection Act

Today's Insurrection Act has four "triggers," or conditions for domestic deployment. Congress provided express language conferring deference for only one: what I refer to as the judicial-proceedings trigger. There is no deference-conferring language in any of the others.  The statutory history supports this reading of the distribution of deference.  In 1792, the Second Congress rejected deferential language in the first Insurrection Act. Congress would revisit the Insurrection Act two more times: in 1861 and in 1871.  In 1861, it granted deference to the one trigger of judicial proceedings. In 1871, it added two new triggers, but without any deference language.

Let's return to the beginning.  In 1792, Congress considered and rejected deferential language before enacting the first Insurrection Act. The first effort to authorize domestic military deployment came as an amendment to a bill regulating the structure of the state militias. The amendment, passed by the Senate in 1792, authorized the president to call out the militia "as the exigence may, in his opinion, require, to execute the laws of the Union, suppress insurrections, and repel invasions." The crucial words were "in his opinion." Because the president's "opinion" modified every trigger for calling out the militia, the amendment would have given the president substantial deference.

The most vehement opponent of the amendment was Representative William Vans Murray, who condemned the legislation because it meant that "the time, the cause, and the place in which the militia were to be called out should be all left to the discretion of one man." This violated the core principle of the Constitution: "a Government of definition, and not of trust and discretion." Murray's objection prevailed. The House rejected the amendment and directed Murray and two other members to prepare a separate bill. The resulting Calling Forth Act contained no comparable language conferring deference on the president in its triggers.

In 1861, Congress added the phrase "in the judgment of the President" to the provision (language that today is phrased "[w]henever the President considers"), but only to the judicial-proceedings trigger, establishing deference in that trigger but nowhere else. That change was understood to settle the controversy over President Lincoln's use of force against the seceding states at the Civil War's outset. By giving him deference, it overturned James Buchanan's argument that the President lacked such authority under the Insurrection Act to fight the Civil War.  When Congress added two new triggers in 1871, it carried no comparable language, leaving the judicial-proceedings trigger as the sole trigger with deference.  The remaining triggers, including "rebellion" and "invasion" which the Ninth Circuit treats as the antecedents for those terms in 10 U.S.C. 12406, had no deference.

Martin v. Mott is a much-discussed 1827 Supreme Court decision interpreting the 1795 Calling Forth Act. The Ninth Circuit read Mott as requiring deference to the president. John Dehn and I, among others, believe this misreads the decision, and the court addresses some of those objections. But my concern here is different: how the statutory history casts Mott in a different light and weakens its force as precedent for interpreting either § 12406 or the Insurrection Act to require deference.

First, Mott interpreted an old version of the Insurrection Act statute, the one from 1795. Congress subsequently amended it extensively, including by adding language conferring deference in 1861 but omitting comparable language when it added new triggers in 1871. § 12406's descends from the amended Insurrection Act, and thus its deference must be read in that light.  Second, two of the triggers in today's Insurrection Act were added only in 1871, decades after Mott was decided. Why should Mott's reasoning extend to them at all?

Finally, Mott addressed the invasion trigger, which is no longer part of the Insurrection Act but is now found in a portion of § 12406 not at issue in Newsom v. Trump. Invasion is one of § 12406's three triggers, alongside rebellion and the inability to execute the laws with regular forces. The Ninth Circuit reasoned that if the invasion trigger requires deference, so too must the other triggers under § 12406. I am skeptical.  But even if the Ninth Circuit is right, that is irrelevant to the Insurrection Act because the invasion trigger is no longer grouped with the other triggers in the Insurrection Act.

The statutory history of the Insurrection Act is extensive, but three developments in 1792, 1861, and 1871 have important implications for deference. Before any court again relies on that history to decide whether, and to what extent, deference is warranted, it must do more than the Ninth Circuit did by merely gesturing at it. It must engage with it. That history, properly understood, casts doubt on granting deference for all but one of the triggers authorizing the president to deploy the military. For the most part, the baseline rule of statutory interpretation remains: Congress has legislated the conditions for domestic deployment, and courts must judge for themselves whether the president has met those conditions without unusual solicitude to a president's views on the matter.

NEXT: U. Colorado Regent-vs.-Regents Lawsuit, Cannabis, Race, and Legislative Immunity

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.

#7794. What Those Little Holes in Your Plug Prongs Are Actually For

Those little holes in electrical plug prongs have a purpose, but it isn't what most people think. Here's why they're still there.

Not all electronic cords look the same. Some have two prongs; others have three or even four. Some have prongs at weird angles, or are even designed for orange electrical outlets. Odds are most people have also seen electrical prongs with holes in them, but the reason for them isn’t common knowledge.

Those two tiny circles often appear near the ends of the metal blades, and newer outlets no longer depend on them. Learn how the feature started, why some manufacturers still use them, what homeowners should know about plug safety, and more.

The holes originally helped keep plugs from slipping out of outlets. Some older outlets had small bumps inside that fit into the holes when someone plugged something in. That changed when Underwriters Laboratories began requiring outlets to hold plugs securely without those bumps.

“Most manufacturers stopped putting the detent nibs on the female contacts, as it made it much harder to meet the maximum force to withdraw and did nothing for the minimum requirement, as the gage had no holes,” according to the National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA).

Basically, the bumps made plugs harder to remove, so manufacturers stopped using them. Today, outlets grip the prongs instead. If a plug starts slipping out, the outlet may need to be replaced. The holes aren’t a child safety feature, either. Tamper-resistant outlets use built-in shutters to keep children from sticking objects inside.

“TRRs work like normal outlets,” according to the Electrical Safety Foundation International. “When you plug into a TRR for the first time, you may be able to feel the internal shutter system engaging. If excessive force is needed to insert a plug into a TRR, there’s a chance that the plug, not the receptacle, is damaged.”

Manufacturers sometimes use the holes to hold the metal prongs in place while making plugs. They don’t help electricity flow through the plug, though. The holes can also hold small safety tags or locks on unplugged appliances. However, these shouldn’t replace proper safety equipment. OSHA also has rules for preventing equipment from accidentally starting during certain types of workplace maintenance.

The holes aren’t even required under American electrical plug standards. Manufacturers can make plugs without them, although NEMA has rules for their size and placement when included. They also have nothing to do with grounding. On a three-prong plug, the round prong handles that job. The two flat prongs work the same way whether they have holes or not.

#7793. Justice Cody Hiland Publicly Criticizes The President For Nominating Him To District Court Instead of Eighth Circuit

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Apparently, the Arkansas Senators are blocking Judge Lee Rudofsky's nomination because Hiland didn't get the nomination.

We are coming into the endgame for President Trump's judicial nominees. Since the election, it seems the President has made (at least) two nominations to the federal bench in Texas: Justice James Sullivan of the Texas Supreme Court for the WDTX seat in Austin and OLC Head Elliot Gaiser for the NDTX seat in Dallas. I say "seems" because the President has not posted these nominations to Truth Social, as that makes it official. But the Senate Judiciary Committee has received questionnaires for both candidates. I have known both of these sharp legal minds for some time, and would welcome their addition to the bench. Will Sullivan and Gaiser get votes? I sure hope so. Over the next six weeks, Republican Senators will need to be motived to vote, while Democrat Senators will pull out every stop to leave these seats open. Plus, there is an entire line of other nominees who are still waiting for votes.

Beyond the district court nominees, there is the question of circuit court nominees. Judge Anna St. John's nomination to the Fifth Circuit and Judge Daniel Domenico's nomination to the Tenth Circuit are pending. They had their hearings some time ago, and should get through. Todd Butler has not even had his hearing yet, so he is down the pecking order. Then there is Judge Lee Rudofksy, a nominee to the Eighth Circuit, who had his hearing back in September. Yet, both of the Arkansas Senators are blocking Rudofsky's nomination. Why? They prefer Justice Cody Hiland, a member of the Arkansas Supreme Court.

There's a problem with Hiland. He has demonstrated absolutely terrible judgment which should permanently disqualify him from holding any public office.

In August, he decided to disclose to a room full of law students private communications between him and the White House Counsel. Worse, rather than teaching students about the value of grace, he promoted belligerence and vindictiveness. In short, the White House approached Hiland about a nomination to the Eighth Circuit. After the vetting process, the White House changed course, and offered Hiland a seat on the federal district court. Hiland refused, and told the White House Counsel to tell President Trump about it. He said all of this on a livestream. You can watch it here, starting around the 16:45 mark:

And I've transcribed the comments for those who prefer to read:

The second thing I want to talk about is you're going to have to learn to be resilient, and maybe this far in your career, maybe it's been easy for you. I don't know, but you're going to have to learn how to be knocked down and then get back up, and then also not to be intimidated. Resiliency is something that is going to carry with you the rest of your career. Now, I'm going to tell you a story that just happened to me because resilience matters even at this point in a career. So, you you want to hear a backstory on something? Nobody ever gets to hear backstories. I'm going to give you a backstory. So, about two months ago, I was contacted about being appointed by the president to the Eighth Circuit. Okay, I had senators who asked me to do it. Applied, went to the interview in front of a White House panel of eight Ivy League attorneys, did an interview, and then got a call. And the call said, "You know what? We're going to recommend that the president appoints you to the Eighth Circuit, and so they started a background check. The FBI goes out, and if you've ever served in these capacities, you know that there's a full field investigation that takes place. And select 12 or 13 agents just investigate you for about six weeks. And in this case, they ask them to finish it in two weeks because they wanted to get it done, and so the FBI went out and they talked to over 130 people about me and my life. And when Dean Crawford is talking about social media, you know that sort of thing matters, okay? Because they go back to the time that you're 18 and they talk to everybody you've ever leased from. They tell you they're going to talk to your girlfriends and everybody else. It's like taking a bath with a brillo pad. Okay, good decisions matter as you go along this course, and so it rocked along. And last Tuesday, I had a meeting. Last Wednesday, I had a meeting for three hours with the Department of Justice, finalizing my Senate Judiciary Committee questionnaire, and it was going to be sent in. And I was told to go home and to expect a phone call from the President of the United States, and to be offered the position. And so I went home and I charged my phone and I called my wife and I said, "You need to come home tonight's the night. We've been through two months of unbelievable minutia of a life that's quite frankly not that interesting. Okay, but I had to have it all, and we had prepared it. It was ready to it was ready to go. And I get a phone call from 202. For those of you don't know, that's Washington D.C. And the man on the other end of the line was not the president of the United States. It was White House Counsel, who, by the way, had recommended that we be chosen. And White House Counsel said the president would like to know if you would be interested in a federal district court position. Eastern District of Arkansas, and I said, "You mean Circuit, Eighth Circuit? No, no, no. Federal District Judge in the Eastern District of Arkansas." And so your mind starts going, "What in the world has happened? What am I hearing?" And so, being belligerent, and at times I said no. That is not a position that I'm interested in. And he came back with after a five second delay of you know not believing what I just said. He said, "So you want me to go back into the Oval Office and tell the President of the United States that you're rejecting an opportunity to be appointed to the federal bench, and I said, "Yes, that's exactly what I want you to tell the president of the United States." And so, you know, I tell that story to say this because I want to be honest. Because too many elected officials are just not transparent, and that happened to me last week. You know what? It's okay because I'd never dreamed of being on the Eighth Circuit. It had never been had come to my mind. But we had an expectation based on an FBI investigation, based on communication from those that make these decisions that it was done. And sometimes, guys, it's not done. Sometimes your expectations are not met. When you're a student here with these kind of people, this kind of quality, not everybody is going to make the top paper. Not everybody is going to make law review. Despite what your expectations may be there are times where your expectations are not going to be met, and it's going to happen for the rest of your life at times. And so, as you begin this career, start developing that resiliency.

Talking to law students is my profession. I can't imagine a judge making such a huge blunder. What lesson are these students taking away here? That you should be so stubborn about getting one position that you refuse another lifetime commission? That you should reveal private communications with the White House in which you admit you were "belligerent"? He is comparing not getting an Eighth Circuit appointment to not getting on law review? No wonder the White House didn't pick him. In my view, making a bad nomination is worse than making no nomination at all (see Butler).  The Eighth Circuit is at a turning point. Judge Stras writes far too many dissents. One more vote could flip the circuit. Arkansas is but one state in the circuit. This stubbornness will spite the good people of those states.

Here's the bottom line. Senators pick Judges who are their friends. Those are the worst possible reasons to pick a judge. We need to reward the people who advance the rule of law, not those who are chummy with Senators. And yes, this applies to Todd Butler too. The Junior Senator from Mississippi told people to choose a different protein. Well, they should have chosen a different judge. But here we are.

#7792. Trial opens for suspect whose multiple email threats include ‘skinning’ federal judge

A series of threatening emails sent to the Northern District of California last year included “skinning U.S. District Judge Charles Breyer” and accused judges from the Golden State of being “enemy combatants.” (Image from Shutterstock)

A series of threatening emails sent to the Northern District of California last year included “skinning U.S. District Judge Charles Breyer” and accused judges from the Golden State of being “enemy combatants.”

David Brooks Pokorny, 45, of El Cerrito, California, allegedly sent 11 email threats in a span of 44 minutes to assault, kidnap and murder Breyer, a senior judge for the Northern District of California, according to U.S. Assistant Attorney Kent Stejskal in opening statements Tuesday.

“Words within those 11 emails constitute what are called true threats,” said Stejskal, according to coverage by Courthouse News Service.

He allowed the 14-person jury to view snippets of the emails during the trial. Pokorny is charged with making felony threats against a judicial officer and faces a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.

According to Pokorny’s public defender John Reichmuth, his client’s words were “truly shocking, truly offensive, truly ugly, but not true threats.”

Reichmuth said the emails were free speech, and the prosecution would have to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Pokorny, who has a history of sending threats to public officials and media outlets, meant to perform the actions described in his emails.

Presiding U.S. District Judge Jon Tigar of the Northern District of California noted that the prosecution does not have to prove that Pokorny intended to carry out the threat for it to supersede the protections of First Amendment free speech rights.

Todd Butler's bare Senate Judiciary Committee Questionnaire.

Todd Butler has now posted his questionnaire for the Senate Judiciary Committee. Here is the chronology Butler offers for his nomination:

On June 29, 2026, Senator Roger Wicker contacted me about a potential vacancy on the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit. I spoke with Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith the following day. On July 1, 2026, an official from the White House Counsel's Office contacted me to arrange an interview. On July 13, 2026, I interviewed with officials from the White House Counsel's Office. Following my interview, I received periodic updates from Senator Wicker about the process. On October I, 2026, President Trump called to inform me that he planned to nominate me for a position on the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit.

There is a very relevant date missing here. On September 28, 2026, Judge Southwick publicly announced that he would take senior status. Yet three months earlier, Senator Wicker contacted Butler about the potential vacancy.

As I said from the outset, the fix was in. There was some sort of deal involving Wicker, Southwick, and the White House. I'm sure this interview was pro forma. and doubt any other candidates were interviewed. Judge Southwick could have announced his intentions at any time in August or early September, but he waited until the last possible moment to jam up the process, and ensure Butler would not go down. I do hope at least one Senator asks Butler if he is aware of any communications in which Judge Southwick, directly or indirectly, conditioned his willingness to take senior status if Butler is the nominee.

As for the rest of the SJQ, let's just say Butler's pantry is bare. Or, the Butler didn't do it.

Butler went to law school between 2005 and 2008, but he wasn't a member of the Federalist Society. That makes sense, as he wrote critically of Justice Scalia, originalism, and the Second Amendment. He wasn't a member while he clerked. Indeed, he didn't become a member of the Federalist Society until 2016. I suspect lots of people joined before or after Trump's victory. It would help with career prospects. He has never held any leadership positions in FedSoc. But rest assured that he was active in the Inn of Court and the Mississippi Bar, holding several leadership positions.

Butler has extensive experience in employment law. In addition to the publications I flagged, Butler speaks and writes often about the EEOC, FLSA, and related topics of municipal law. His only professional exposure to constitutional law involves defendant local officials who are sued for violating First Amendment rights. After Olivier v. City of Brandon, his most significant case was as defense counsel in a wrongful death case. He taught at the Mississippi College of Law "periodic[ally]" between 2008 and 2016 but does not recall which semesters he taught. He also does not have copies of the syllabi.

Here is how Butler describes his pro bono work:

Over the course of my career, I have accepted pro bono clients, typically through the Mission First Legal Aid Clinic or the Mississippi Volunteers Lawyers Project. I have assisted with adoptions, child visitation matters, and other domestic issues. I also have provided pro bono services to a local church, including contract review and procedure drafting, in connection with the operation of a faith-based children's center. I advised a local pastor on a land acquisition that he is considering using for a fellowship facility. And I have volunteered, along with others at my law firm, at Stewpot Community Services, where we served meals to people experiencing homelessness.

There is no pro bono work that would remotely be associated with the conservative legal movement. And no, working for a church does not necessarily make a person conservative.

If I were to show you this questionnaire, without any knowledge of Mississippi politics, would you possibly think this was a viable record for the Fifth Circuit? No.
